TITANIUM
speechtext:
1.	What quantity of titanium is exported each year by Canada to the United States, and at what price?
2.	What quantity of titanium is imported each year by Canada from the United States after treatment, and at what price?
3.	What percentage of the titanium imported from the United States has previously been exported from Canada?
4.	Are there any reduction plants in Canada?
5.	If not, how many reduction plants would be needed to prevent importation and meet the requirements of the Canadian industry?
6.	How much would it cost approximately to build such plants?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TITANIUM
speechtext:
It is not possible to answer this question in the form in which it is asked.
There are no integrated plants for producing titanium metal or other titanium bearing products from titanium ore in Canada.
One company is developing a large ilmenite deposit at Allard lake on the north shore of the lower St. Lawrence river. This company has a reduction plant at Sorel, Quebec, which will process this ore to recover pig iron and a high titanium bearing slag which will be shipped to the United States for processing into titanium oxide. As yet the company has only one furnace in operation and the operation has not proceeded beyond the pilot plant stage. Any shipments of titanium slag can as yet only be regarded as experimental to determine its amenability to treatment by the existing American plants.
Imports from the United States of titanium bearing products are in the form of titanium oxide for the paint and pigment industry and as ferro-titanium for ferro-alloying industry. A small amount of the imported
Questions
titanium oxide is converted into titanium metal, by Dominion Magnesium Company, of Renfrew, Ontario, and the major part of this metal is exported to the United States. As only one company is making titanium metal, figures of production are not available for publication.
Imports of titanium oxide are of the order of 15,000 tons a year, valued in excess of three million dollars. Approximately 500 tons of ferro-titanium of 25 per cent grade are consumed in Canada annually.
No actual estimate of the cost of erecting a plant capable of meeting Canadian demands for titanium dioxide is available.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Information I have received suggests it might be of interest to the house and to the people of Canada to know what arrangements are being made for the supplying to our armed forces in Korea and elsewhere, of Canadian cigarettes and other Canadian products of the kind which they would commonly use.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I am glad of the opportunity
extended by the question of the leader of the opposition to say something about this matter. In the first place, it may be pointed out that the Canadian brigade group now forms a part of the first United Nations- commonwealth-division. The supplies for this group are furnished, like those for the other commonwealth forces, from United States sources. It would not be economical for us to have a separate supply line.
We do have the service of No. 426 squadron carrying special supplies, including mail and other amenities, to the Far East for our forces. Under existing arrangements Canadian cigarettes can be purchased from one of the manufacturers by residents in Canada and shipped by mail, tax free, to individual personnel in the theatre of operations. I understand that these arrangements are well worked out, and that shipments are rapid.
In the second place, it is also possible for Canadian cigarettes to be purchased by Canadian personnel through their own paymaster, but the supplies have to be forwarded from Canada. We are endeavouring to make arrangements whereby cigarettes, in addition to the supplies of other peculiarly Canadian products desired by the troops, will be immediately available out of stores arranged with the United Kingdom or United States authorities. If necessary, we shall set up our special Canadian agencies.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
Hon. members might be interested in a brief comment I received in a letter from a number of men who are serving in Korea which indicates that there may be reasons why civilian organizations could do something in this respect. The letter indicates that some of these cigarettes were being sent

to me-and I may say to the member for Fort William that I have not smoked them.
I quote one paragraph:
We are enclosing a sample ol some of the cigarettes we get. I believe you will agree with us as to their quality. We figure that if we keep smoking then we will all be back in Canada by the time our throats recover.
I know that is written in a humorous way, Mr. Speaker, and I welcome the explanation. It might be well if Canadians generally realized that it will be of considerable assistance to our troops overseas if civilian organizations do something about forwarding Canadian cigarettes and other things of that type to which the men are accustomed.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I quite agree, Mr. Speaker. I believe the hon. member has sufficiently described the cigarettes in question to indicate that they are not Canadian. As a matter of fact, we have had a number of officers out there to make arrangements of this kind. We have to work with our friends in the United States and Great Britain in this regard, and they are very co-operative. It is a long way off, though. We hope to arrive at a satisfactory solution of the problem.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO SUPPLYING CANADIAN CIGARETTES TO PERSONNEL ON ACTIVE SERVICE

speechtext: I do not know. We shall have to look into that.

There are just one or two points which I feel should be put on record at this time. We have voted $5 billion for defence to be spent over the next three years. This is a large sum of money, but it is an important thing for us to do because we must keep our country secure in times like these. However, one of several things

could happen. We may be in the middle of a war before the three years are up, or we may have reached some sort of amicable settlement with our potential enemies, in which event there would be little likelihood of war. Should the situation continue as it is now, the things that we have been building with the money we have been spending would no doubt be becoming obsolete, and the expenditures made on them would have to be repeated. If we continue to tax ourselves as we are doing, and if we have to continue to put all our energies into this type of thing for the next twenty or thirty years, our potential enemy, communism, will have won its point. It would break us financially. If we could make our position safe through the NATO organization and the efforts we are making ourselves, then we would defeat our potential enemy, communism, provided that we could continue to develop our own country along with what we are doing in matters of defence. In manufactures we are well developed, but in agriculture there are certain things that are likely to suffer. But there is one project which has been considered by the federal government, and on which it has spent a great deal of time and money, that I hope will not be delayed because of the situation in which we find ourselves today. I refer to the South Saskatchewan river project.
People in Ontario, where there is all this beautiful greenery, rivers and all the amenities of summer life, probably do not realize what the condition of the country is around Outlook and south of Saskatoon. People are trying to grow wheat and field crops under very adverse conditions. Many areas do not produce enough to give them a living, and we in this House of Commons are faced with such things as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and direct relief. I have some figures on how much money has been put into this kind of thing. In the area I believe some $42 million have been put into relief and some $14 million into P.F.A. Instead of the federal government putting out money in this way, had some sort of irrigation development been carried on, had the government assisted in the erection of the dam, the result would have been a real capital asset to the people of Canada.
I hope the chairman will not mind if I quote extensively from information that has been compiled by the Department of Agriculture, because it gives a good many figures, and I should like to have them right on the record. The capital cost of this whole project will be about $103,700,000. The sum of $68,600,000 would go to the actual construction of the dam itself and the reservoir. The irrigation distribution system would cost
Supply-Agriculture
about $19,500,000; land improvement, and deficit period-that is, the period until it starts to operate-$5,600,000; and the power plant that would supply the power would cost $10 million.
It has been proposed that the federal government put into this project $68,600,000, to impound the water and construct the dam and the works that necessarily go with it. This expenditure would be spread over a period of ten years. In the first few years the cost would be low, but it would be accelerated toward the end when the major works were installed. The province and the farmers would pay the balance of $35,100,000. It should be remembered that the engineers of the federal government have determined that this project would be feasible. They have investigated it, and they know it will work. The investigation cost us a lot of money.
The government of the province of Saskatchewan seemed to doubt whether the project would be feasible, but I understand that they have now decided they can go into it and that it will be a real asset to the people. They are prepared to lay out the money. The power plant, to cost $10 million, will be built by the province, and they will take the power. Also the province will complete the irrigation works, at a cost of another $25 million. The water stored would provide irrigation for 500,000 acres, of which 431,000 are good irrigable land. The population would be increased tremendously on that type of land, and the assurance of a decent livelihood would be increased tremendously as well.
There is a sufficient flow of water to develop 375 million kilowatt hours of energy, firm-that is, firm power that could be guaranteed; and another 100 million of secondary energy at times when the water flow is high.
The industrial life of Saskatchewan has been impeded owing to the fact that we did not have the plant to produce enough power to give industry all the power it needed. With this project we would have plenty of power. The provincial authorities, through the power commission, say that they could use that power.
The irrigation system itself would increase the number of farmers on this area from 1,245 to 2,700. On this basis it is expected that the irrigation system itself would meet the cost of operation. The power commission, on the other hand, would value the firm energy at some 5J mills and the secondary energy at 3 mills at the dam site. The gross value would be $2,088,000, and the net value $1,300,000. These facts leave no doubt that the irrigation and the power plant would carry themselves.

The climate around the area to be irrigated is very much the same as it is in the Lethbridge irrigation district, where the irrigation cost was $57 an acre. The province of Alberta attempted to carry it in a kind of co-operative way, I believe, without too much success, because the increase in produce and the power would not be enough to pay the expenses. The $57 an acre could not be borne by the farmers; therefore in order to make the project possible it will be necessary for the federal government to put up enough money to create this reservoir. Under the P.F.A. legislation it has been pretty well decided that it is the federal government's job to impound the water, provided that the water is used.
The Meek report indicates some of the changes in the country around this irrigation project, the St. Mary storage project. It says:
In 1924, when the Lethbridge northern district was first irrigated, there were only about 300 families in the area. Now about 900 families occupy farms on the project.
Where these people formerly lived was semi-arid country. Now they are living in a country that has trees, flowers and community life. They are living close together. They are farming more intensively, and their lives are more or less comparable to life on farms around Ottawa where there is plenty of moisture. The community advantages resulting from irrigation deserve special emphasis. The report goes on:
The social and community advantages resulting from irrigation deserve special emphasis, though these benefits can only be partly indicated statistically. These advantages were observed by the committee on all projects visited, and a good example is found in the Lethbridge northern irrigation district. Here an area of some 360 square miles, equivalent to ten townships, has been transformed in less than two decades from sparsely settled prairie, subject to periodical crop failures and soil drifting, to a thriving community of farm homes, towns and villages.
In less than two decades the area has been transformed from the kind of conditions I have been describing to the kind that you see around this city. The population increased from 1,500 to 10,000, thereby making it possible to improve the schools and to establish rural electrification, and for the people to have all the other things that make life on the farm more pleasant.
It is unthinkable that a project such as this should not be proceeded with. I will admit that it is costly. But if you take a year at a time, a few millions of dollars each year would transform that whole area from a semi-arid region into one of which Canada could be proud.
There is another point I should like to stress. As Canada developed it was found

necessary to develop the west, and as the west developed, Canada became a greater nation. There have been many complaints about our talking about wheat; but when it is realized that we send out of the country each year 300 million bushels of wheat and bring back the money-nearly half a billion dollars-to the farms in the western provinces, where there is very little manufacturing, and when we know that nearly all that money eventually goes to industries in central Canada,, we appreciate the importance of western Canada to the rest of the country.
The development of the west has been an important factor in the industrial development of central Canada-indeed in the entire development of this country as a nation. I would urge that this project be given the go-ahead signal immediately, so that we may open our arms to more of the world's population. On the basis of this project alone, we could probably double the population in Saskatchewan within twenty-five years. I do not see how anyone could urge that a project such as this should be delayed. All such developments should be proceeded with immediately.

Mr. Chairman, I join with the two hon. members who have spoken in support of a project that is necessary, agriculturally, to the survival of central Saskatchewan. This matter has been argued on previous occasions, and the facts have been recapitulated by the hon. member for Kindersley. Without regard to party considerations or strife, all of us from Saskatchewan are united in the demand that this work be proceeded with.
The population of Saskatchewan has been decreasing for the last twelve or fifteen years. In considerable measure that decrease is due to drought and crop failure.

And the C.C.F.
government.

Well, I never like to place so heavy a responsibility upon any government. I have been trying to deal with the matter entirely apart from considerations of that kind.
This project is necessary to the future not only of Saskatchewan, but of Canada as a whole. Industry will not be decentralized as it should be unless power is developed in agricultural areas. In Saskatchewan we have available for development hundreds of thousands of horsepower. We have before us the example of the government of the United States, which in recent years has endeavoured to instil into its people the realization of a need for the decentralization of industry.
Without industrial development in Saskatchewan we begin to wonder how our population will be maintained. As the hon. member for Kindersley said, from time to time, from as far back as 1775, when the first records were available, vast areas have been almost denuded of crops as a result of drought conditions in the southeasterly section of the province, extending from Saskatoon.
This piece of work is necessary in the interests of the industrialization of Saskatchewan. It is necessary to provide an assured and continuing agricultural income. It has been found feasible, and it will be self-liquidating. It will assure a development never before experienced in Saskatchewan, and will pay dividends in national development.
I wish to deal with farm income in 1950 as it affected not only my own province but the dominion as a whole. The incomes of
Supply-Agriculture
Canadian farmers went down to $271 million less than they were in 1949. Cash income in Saskatchewan in 1950 was $407,600,000 as compared with $560,700,000 in 1949, or a drop of $153 million. In considerable measure that decreased income in Saskatchewan is the result of climatic conditions the effect of which would have been considerably if not entirely removed if this irrigation plan and power development on the South Saskatchewan river had been proceeded with.
In Alberta, farm income fell during the year by $92 million, and in Manitoba by $46,800,000. I rise for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the minister a question that is of prime importance to western farmers and concerns the prosperity of the country as a whole. I realize that the marketing of farm products, including wheat, is the responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but the production of those commodities is the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture. Over 200 million bushels of wheat are being marketed under the international wheat agreement. At the present time the price paid under that agreement is about 37 cents less per bushel than the wheat board is receiving from the sales elsewhere of class II wheat. The loss has already run into $10 million, and it is bound to increase if the world remains as it is today, in a state of three-quarters peace or, as described by the London Economist, as a world of fear wherein wheat as a major commodity of sustenance will become in greater demand. The present disparity of 37 cents between the price under the international wheat agreement and what the farmer would otherwise receive is likely to increase if the demand continues, with a correspondingly greater loss to the western farmer.
The international wheat agreement contains a provision for revision of prices upward under certain -circumstances. All the signatories to the agreement are nations which have joined together to meet the onrush of communism. All realize that there can be no assured unity until all the peoples of the nations joined together in this effort are -united and have a high morale. There -is a provision in the agreement for the prices that will prevail during the next few years. In
1950-	51 the maximum price will be $1.80; in
1951-	52 the maximum price will be $1.80, and there will be the same maximum price in
1952-	53, when the agreement will end. In 1952-53 the minimum, as compared with today's minimum price fixed under the agreement, is 20 cents lower than the first year's minimum price.
With other hon. members I have urged the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make

Supply-Agriculture
application to the nations signatory to this agreement with a view to securing an upward revision of prices. Unless there is such a revision, the wheat farmer is going to become more and more disgruntled as the days go by and the price of class II wheat increases, provided that world conditions continue in their present fearful state.
The international wheat agreement contains a provision which I believe allows for a revision upward or downward as the case may be. Article VI deals with prices, and section 5 of that article reads:
5. If any exporting or importing country represents to the executive committee that any price equivalent established under paragraph 2, 3, or 4 of this article is,-[DOT]
Those are the paragraphs which establish the price equivalents for bulk wheat:
-in the light of current transportation or exchange rates or market premiums or discounts, no longer fair, the executive committee shall consider the matter and may, in consultation with the advisory committee on price equivalents, make such adjustment as it considers advisable.
I submit that since the agreement was entered into in 1950 there have been increases in transportation costs in Canada; there have been increases in freight rates and also in other costs which might be considered by the executive committee in deciding whether or not an adjustment should be made. I realize that the Minister of Agriculture is not in a position to act because of the portfolio he holds, but I urge him to appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on behalf of the Canadian people to make an application for a revision upward. Conditions cannot go on as they are, the farmer being faced with increasing costs of production while being required to sell his wheat at a price that as time goes on will represent less and less profit under the international wheat agreement.
The answer given the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was that there were thirty-seven importing countries and only three exporting countries which were signatories to the agreement. I believe that if those forty countries, whether exporting or importing, are as anxious as we are to mobilize to the utmost in order to preserve ourselves against the potential communist challenge, they would toe just as anxious as we are to do everything possible to remove any injustices under that international agreement.
The Minister of Agriculture represents a western constituency, and I know he is desirous that prosperity be maintained on the prairies, without which there cannot be any Canadian prosperity. I ask him to use his prestige and influence upon the Minister

of Trade and Commerce in an effort to have him do what up to the present he has not shown any desire to do. Indeed, he adopted the attitude, when asked a question about this matter, that there was no use in doing anything, because after all one would be too optimistic to believe that anything could be done.
The Canadian dollar has fallen considerably in purchasing power since the agreement was entered into. I have not the exact' figures, but, speaking from memory, at the time the agreement was entered into the index for Canadian commodity prices was about 160, whereas today it is approximately 180. There has been a pronounced increase in the cost of the commodities which the farmer must buy. This is a matter that transcends any political considerations in the western provinces. As I see it, it is a matter that demands a united front on the part of all the western provinces to the end that at least an application be made for revision. Whether or not action can be forced we do not know, but we can at least try.
Surely we have the right to ask that the Minister of Trade and Commerce shall not be permitted to stand in the way of what would be fair and just. There is not a farmer in Alberta, Manitoba or Saskatchewan to whom I have spoken who is not in favour of an upward revision in prices. The time is now, not in 1953, when the agreement will be concluded. We must take action now if we are to assure the maintenance of a high degree of production, which, as I see it, cannot be done unless the morale of the western farmer is kept up. If that morale is to be maintained he must have at least the hope that something definite will be done to revise upward the price of wheat under the international wheat agreement.
When that agreement was made, many felt that it was an excellent thing, for it assured a degree of security. At that time no one could have predicted just how serious the world situation would become; and it is getting more serious day by day. Having regard to the changed circumstances I feel that the Minister of Agriculture should join hon. members in all parts of this house from the western provinces-and we have always received the support of the east when we have had a just case-to insist that something be done to the end that prices toe placed upon a basis that is fair and just to Canadian wheat farmers.

Before discussing the main topic in which I am interested I should like to associate myself with the remarks just made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Certainly the people of Saskatchewan believe

that a request should be made to have wheat prices under the international wheat agreement revised upward. It may be that the purchasing countries concerned will not agree, but certainly no harm would be done by attempting an upward revision.
I should like also to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Kinders-ley. During this session I have been pleased to hear a large number of members from [DOT]Saskatchewan on the government side speak in favour of the South Saskatchewan irrigation project. It is something we in this party, together with hon. members of other parties, have been advocating for many years. This afternoon the people of Saskatchewan are waiting anxiously for the remarks the Minister of Agriculture will probably make in a few minutes, indicating whether or not the project will be proceeded with this year. There have been rumours and newspaper reports that the cabinet has been discussing the matter, and that the minister has been trying to sell his colleagues on the project. I hope he has been successful, because, as I said a moment ago, there is nothing more needed in Saskatchewan today.
I was speaking to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle the other day, just after he had returned from the west. He told me that last week the dust was blowing so thick you could hardly see. In the plane in which he was travelling ten or twelve people were ill as a result of the high winds; and of course at this time of year in the dust bowl when the wind is high the dust is very bad. Often at this time of year I have driven out in my car and have been unable to see beyond the engine. Frequently you have to drive with your lights on in the middle of the day. This irrigation project would not change that completely, of course, but certainly it would go a long way toward alleviating it.
I am not going into the advantages of the project; everyone in this house knows them. If anything is needed to give our province stability, it is this irrigation project. I know of nothing else in Canada today, with the possible exception of the St. Lawrence waterway development, which is more important or which deserves greater consideration from this house.
I was interested in reading some old Hansards the other night to see the reasons that have been advanced since I have been in parliament for not proceeding with the South Saskatchewan development. I realize that no one wants this project more than the Minister of Agriculture, but either he has not been able to sell it to his colleagues, or something has always happened to prevent its commencement. In 1946 the reason given for

not proceeding was the shortage of men and materials. In 1947 the lack of progress was blamed on inability to locate a suitable dam site. In 1948 the reason was that eastern members had to be sold on the project. Last year the reason was unique; the minister made the statement that we must have assurance from somebody that an organization would be set up to utilize the water and to pay a share of the cost sufficient to ensure that they would take some responsibility for seeing that the work is carried on. Then he went on to point out that the provincial government should bear a share of the cost. Up to that time I had never heard the suggestion that the province would have to pay part of the cost, and I think that was a harsh proposal, in view of the financial position of Saskatchewan. Nevertheless our provincial government has now agreed to that plan and is willing to bear roughly one-third of the cost; I believe it has indicated that fact to the minister. Therefore I can see no reason why something should not be done this year. After all, we are going to spend $3,700 million this year. Surely it should not be hard to find the $10 million that is needed to get this project started.
I remember that in one of his speeches out west the minister said we could make this area of Saskatchewan the Essen of Canada; and if that could be done, no one would be more delighted than I. That statement was made just before an election, but still I think it was a reasonable thing to say, and something which could be accomplished. I believe the citizens of Saskatchewan and the west generally, whether they be Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F.'ers or Social Crediters, will be disappointed if the minister gets up today and tells us that, in view of our defence and other needs, once again this much needed undertaking will have to be postponed. The excuse that men and materials are not available will no longer suffice. That is the reason we were given back in 1946, and it seems to me if such an excuse is given today we shall be going around in a vicious circle. If we do not proceed at once, and war should come, we may go on for decades without getting this development. Therefore I hope the minister will announce that it is to be proceeded with at once.

In connection with the development of the South Saskatchewan project, I want to indicate how the neighbours of that province feel about that development. We in southern Alberta have witnessed the transformation that can be made through the proper use of irrigation. I lived in a very dry area where we were never certain of crop returns at any time. My father was

Supply-Agriculture
among those who developed the first irrigation system in our province, the old Alberta railway and irrigation system, and I recall the many weeks he was away from home working on that project. I mention this only because I want to convey to hon. members the fact that I have witnessed the change that can be brought about when water is made available. I saw that dry section of the country become almost a beautiful garden; and I also saw the coffers of the provincial and federal governments enriched by the returns from that land which produced more abundantly than ever before. When I think of what happened in southern Alberta, and when I think also of the present situation in the province of Saskatchewan, our sister province, I cannot help but express my hope that the government of Canada will find it possible to lend a substantial hand in the building of the dam across the South Saskatchewan river so as to provide the much needed water for those parched and thirsty lands in Saskatchewan. I am certain that if the federal government does so that inhabitants of the sister province of Alberta will support the effort. I feel that wherever worthy projects of this kind can be seen, it should not matter in what province the development is to take place. We, as Canadians, must look at it as Canadians. I am speaking now I think for the people of the province of Alberta when I say that we welcome the development of water resources for the province of Saskatchewan. We will certainly give financial support, through taxation measures or any others that need be, to see that that development takes place.
I recall, Mr. Chairman, while I was in the provincial government quite a number of years ago now, along with some of my colleagues, taking the first step towards the conservation of the east slope of the Rockies in order that we might conserve our water resources and make it possible for the province of Saskatchewan-possibly western Manitoba-to have a share in the run-off waters from these slopes. Serious Are hazards had beset these areas for many years. Some of them had been almost denuded' of trees, and we were not certain whether there would be water. I believe it was about 1937 I came down and discussed the matter with officials of the federal government with a view to establishing some form of co-operation between the province and the dominion so that we could conserve the forests on the east slope of the watershed. I am pleased to say, Mr. Chairman, that the federal government came to realize the importance of that conservation. They did set up the Eastern Rockies forest conservation board, which is

doing a fine job. They have made it possible for the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan- perhaps some in Manitoba-to be assured of water resources in the future. Not only did that commission take steps to conserve the watershed, but it decided upon a division of the waters as between Alberta and Saskatchewan. With that division assured, it seems to me that the next step ought to be the development of a dam and reservoir so that the people of Saskatchewan might be able to realize what we have already realized in a good many areas in Alberta, that we can have abundant production in those sunny areas with the rich soil if we can get the water. I join with the member for Kindersley, and others who have spoken, in expressing the hope the federal government will see its way clear to doing something towards the development of water resources in the province of Saskatchewan at an early date.
I now wish, Mr. Chairman, to say a word about this question of the international wheat agreement. I do not expect to go into that too fully at the moment. I would say that the member for Lake Centre made a pertinent and reasonable request. Now is the time to ask for a review of the whole agreement. I should not like to see the same thing happen with respect to the international wheat agreement as happened in connection with the British wheat agreement. If we leave it too long, however, there is likely to develop much the same dissatisfaction amongst the farmers of Canada. I must say right here, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers of western Canada that are affected by this long-term agreement are not asking for anything unreasonable when they ask for a revision, because world wheat prices, at least in some cases, are thirty-eight cents above the international wheat agreement price. That means, of course, that the farmers of the country, when they are forced to sell most of their wheat under the international wheat agreement at a figure that represents a considerable loss, feel that now is the time to ask for an upward revision.
Then, one should remember that the farmers of Canada, who number not more than twenty-five or twenty-seven per cent of the total population of this country, are today still making it possible for the Canadian people to have cheaper bread than they would have if the wheat were all sold at world prices, or somewhat above the international wheat agreement figure.' The farmers are selling to the millers of Canada at a rate that means that the farmers, one-third of the population, are subsidizing cheap bread for the rest of the population of Canada. That

situation ought not to exist. It was true all during the time the British wheat agreement was in force, and the farmers of Canada lost not less than $48 million. Many people, of course, believe they lost a good many millions more than that. The important thing is that this is the time to ask for a review of the agreement, and as the member for Lake Centre said, to ask for some upward revision of the price.
On going into supply on May 1 I raised the whole question of the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I pointed out particularly some ways in which the administration of that act was discriminating against certain farmers in the Peace River country. Lands that are not marginal but perfectly good farm lands, and which in normal years would produce a good crop, last year were subjected to two very tragic events. In the first place a wide strip of the country was riddled with hail, and the crops did not recover because it came too late in the season. Then, we were visited with a heavy frost early in the season, with the result that in a large part of the country the yields from the lands were below what would be necessary to qualify for a prairie farm assistance payment.
Now, because many of these farmers hold land under what is called a crown lease agreement, as a result of the amendment which was put through this house in 1950 they are prevented from getting benefits under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I am sure I do not need to review the situation for the minister. He was here the day I spoke about it. I am just asking the minister if he would indicate, when he speaks, whether or not it would be possible to make some change in the act, so as to enable these farmers who are holding leases on the ten-year term to get benefits from the act. Each year they are paying their one per cent contribution, and they feel that they have been discriminated against in this last year because they were barred from any of the benefits under the act.

Mr. Chairman, owing to the geographical position of my constituency I could hardly be expected to keep silent during the course of this debate. I shall not add much to it in the way of argument because I believe the matter has been discussed time and again in committees like this. It has been discussed time and again in my hearing by the Minister of Agriculture in his various speeches throughout the province of Saskatchewan. I am thinking particularly of the time when I began to take more interest in those things, probably back in 1944, and I

remember quite vividly some of his speeches. I have referred to some of them on a previous occasion in this chamber. I do not want in any way to taunt the minister in regard to what one might consider to be breach of promise in regard to this particular construction. I believe it is probably true, as we have heard today, that the minister has been pressing for the construction of this particular dam. As someone else has done, I shall say that I hope that is a fact and that in his effort he will be successful.
This is not a party matter, Mr. Chairman. I should like to congratulate my friend the hon. member for Kindersley upon his speech and upon his approach to the matter in this chamber. The hon. member for Moose Jaw has, I think, disposed of most of the arguments which have been advanced against the construction of this dam. I have said something about the geographical situation of my own city. I might supplement that by saying this, and I think it is perhaps more true in the west than it is in the east, particularly in the part of the west from which I come: the prosperity of the people in the city-not only businessmen but workers-depends upon the prosperity of the farmers, not necessarily those in the immediate vicinity but those even a long distance away, because distances in those provinces are great.
There is something sentimental about the way in which prairie dwellers look upon the matter of water. Down in the east here, people do not think too much about water because, I suppose, they get too much of it; at least, that is my own impression. The Saskatchewan river wends its slow way along, not far distant from where I live in the city of Saskatoon. My hon. friends from the east may have some difficulty in believing it, but on every fair summer Sunday afternoon- and we have many of them in that province -long rows of cars draw up along the north end of Spadina crescent and simply sit there in order to watch the water running over the dam. That dam might seem to have no specific use and people often wondered why it was built. My own impression is that it was built partially at least to give relief work back in the years of depression. At any rate, it is there and it is a little bit of running water and it adds to the beauty of our city. Saskatchewan people like to look at running water.
There are so many stories about drought that I am almost tempted to tell one or two- some of them are humorous-but I think perhaps it would be wasting the time of the committee. I am interested in irrigation and I am interested in what my friend the hon. member for Peace River has said about

Supply-Agriculture
Alberta. One of the first jobs I ever had in Canada-and I think it was back in 1910, if I remember aright-was driving a team of horses and a scraper on an irrigation ditch which was being constructed out of the Bow river in the province of Alberta somewhere -I am not sure of the vicinity-near the village of Brant not far from Strathmore where the Canadian Pacific Railway people had that fine herd of Holstein cows. I do not know whether or not they have it there now. I am thinking now about our own people looking at water and the influence which it has, or which the lack of it has, in our lives on the prairies. I remember those Indian braves, on their way to the stampede. I was not fortunate; I could not go to the stampede because I had to drive my team with a plow breaking up one of the quarter sections which the Canadian Pacific Railway sold as ready-made farms or under some such title to Americans. The people of the United States were so enamoured of the success of irrigation in their own country that when they were able to come up into Canada and when they were offered land at $75 an acre- they said: Is this land irrigated? Irrigated land at $75 an acre?-they were prepared to buy it. I hope they made out well on their investment. I often wondered about the success of that project, because they were breaking land, some of which was fairly rough; and I was wondering how the grain would ripen in the bottom of the valley as compared with that on the tops of the hills in the same section.
I remember as I was plowing along there, with six horses on a gang plow at that particular time, I used to watch those Indians from the Blackfoot reserve pass on their way to the Calgary stampede, and boylike, I envied them. I noticed how they would camp alongside the irrigation ditch. Those Indian braves would often stand on one foot-I do not know why-with a bright blanket around their shoulders, while the ladies in the tribe -that is not the name we generally use- would unload the. democrats, light the fire and proceed to prepare supper. I envied the Indian braves for that, because I had to cook my own supper.
Perhaps that is enough of reminiscence. I merely want to say that we in the west love water. We go to it on every possible occasion. Prairie people, when they go for a holiday or a week-end vacation, go to a lake. Unfortunately we are obliged to go farther and farther in order to get to our lakes because the water level-largely owing to our own foolishness, I think-is becoming lower and lower; and on the bed of many of

the lakes which I knew as a boy, and on which I shot ducks as a boy, oats are now being grown; and the tourist business in that particular district at least is no more.
I think one would have great temerity to say that the greatest problem the world is faced with is not that of world peace. I had better not say that, because it is a statement that might be challenged in various quarters. But I will say that an equally great problem is that of growing food for the people of the nations of the world. I do not think that we can expect to live on this island of security here where plenty of land is available for the growing of food while at the same time thousands of people are starving in other parts of the world.
You know, we are a wasteful people. I think of ourselves in the west. I have seen a Prince Edward Island farmer come out there, take a look at the way we drive around our fields and sometimes drive the binder close to the fence; we do not even bother coming back upon it. He will say to us "You fellows waste more grain than we would grow on our whole farm".
It occurs to me that there are small acreages of wild land all across this country which European people or Oriental people would be delighted to use. For instance, the Greeks can be seen coming down from the mountains with their mules, with the pannier on each side filled with lemons and oranges grown on a half-acre patch somewhere up on the side of the mountain. Or you can go to the hills of Scotland, or to my native Ireland, and you will find people walking along there, plowing with one horse on a slope where they could not use two, walking in the space between the stones, plowing those little fields no bigger than this chamber, hedged around with piles of stone that through the centuries they have picked off the land. Farming under those conditions is subsistence farming, it is true; but at least it is a subsistence, and many of the peoples of the world have not that.
I suggest that one of our greatest problems is how we are to grow food for the increasing population of the world. That takes me back to Saskatchewan. I think the greatest problem in Saskatchewan is the tendency to depopulate that province through the mechanization of farm operations. I am not suggesting that we should go back to the two-horre team or to the walking plow. We must advance. We cannot turn the clock of progress back, but we have to change something, because the population in these western provinces-I mean the prairie provinces-is tending to decrease. I do not

mean that it is decreasing over-all, but the farm population is decreasing because fewer and fewer men are needed to farm those acres. I remember when we used to thresh, and I am sure the minister has seen lots of outfits that I could describe with their old Reeves steam engine, which used to have a twenty-six man crew, a cook, a bull cook, strawboss, stook team men, spike pitchers and field pitchers, twenty-six or more men in all. Did I hear the minister interject?

I was just saying to the
hon. member for Fort William that he and I used to fire the engine.

Yes, with straw, no doubt,
I have not done that job, but I have done most of the others. The point I want to make is that it took anywhere from twenty-four to thirty-two men to do the work that an old man and a boy-and by the way most of the farmers in Saskatchewan are pretty old in their average years-can do today. As a matter of fact, they can do more work than the whole of us did years ago all put together. What does it mean in the life of a province; what does it mean in the life of the population? Here you have a great new province with thousands and thousands of miles of roads to be developed. How are they to be developed? Only through the payment of taxes, only by population. You have your schools to run, and all the rest of it. We have just about reached the limit of the depopulation of the country through mechanization, and if we are to restore that population, or restore any of it, we have to get a different type of farming. Well, somebody says that we have relied on farm mechanized straight grain farming. We have been told for years that we should go into mixed farming. Down in this eastern part of the country and in Prince Edward Island they say:	Well, you crazy
people in Saskatchewan do not even keep a milch cow. The minister and some of the others of us know why we do not keep a milch cow in certain districts. We have seen, as I saw in 1933, a man coming home in his buggy with one bale of hay in the back of the buggy to keep the one surviving cow alive, the others having been shot because there was nothing for them to eat.
I do not want to paint that as being a picture of ordinary conditions in the province of Saskatchewan, but those conditions have occurred and they may occur again. There is a good deal of land in the Palliser triangle where you may graze a few head of cattle on a quarter-section in the summertime, but you cannot be assured of winter forage for them there.
Supply-Agriculture
The experience of irrigation in Alberta near Lethbridge, I think it is, where the beet industry has started up and where beef steers are fed proves that if we had something like that in Saskatchewan it would at least provide winter forage for such cattle as we could graze in the summertime.
I do not think that this good market, this increase in the price of beef, is altogether a transitory thing. I think we may have it with us for some years to come. Irrigation would be a great encouragement to the cattle industry.
There are other problems of course. There is the question of flood control. We have abused the natural resources which we have. Our lands in places are becoming eroded. We have cut down the timber in the north which preserved the water level, and we have a situation of flooding in spring which has become all over this country a pretty serious matter. Just to the south of my own city we have what used to be a lake. It is no longer a lake in anything except name. It is called Pike lake. By the way, it used to be a summer resort, and it was only a few miles away. Now we have to go 175 miles or more to find good water. The farms in this area become flooded every year, and sometimes it is just touch and go whether the flood will subside in time so that the farmers will be able to put crops in. Again we have south of my city two or three little experiments in irrigation. Water is pumped out of the Saskatchewan river and ditched through the co-operation of one of the minister's divisions, the provincial government and the municipal authorities. These ditches can be damaged seriously by the effect of a flood.
I am told that one of the results of a properly controlled irrigation water development scheme in Saskatchewan would be to lessen the chance of those districts being flooded.
I have talked longer than I had intended to, because I had prepared absolutely nothing on the matter, but simply rose to endorse the arguments which have been advanced by other hon. members. I should like to take the position that this is not simply a plea for something which would assist in my own city, much as it would do that; nor is it just a plea for something which will help my own province, much as it would do that. I think it has reached the stage where this thing has become a national project, and I would plead with the minister, if that is necessary, to use that great influence he has upon his colleagues so that they may do something about it.

We may say that something is being done, ft is true that surveys have been made there. Some reference has been made to elections. I have to be honest and say that before the last election there was a certain amount of activity. There were cars driving around there and surveyors were there. I am not saying that there was any connection between the two.
They are still there.

They were there, and I am glad they are there still. I presume they have largely done their work now. I do not know what the next step is. I do know that, so far as any actual work which would mean the production of water for those parched lands is concerned, nothing has been done. In other words, no sod has been turned in that particular irrigation project. I know about the preliminaries, and I know about the surveys. What we want is to get something done. I know that the provincial government, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw has said, and I agree with him-I think they were offered a rather hard deal in the matter-has at least risen to the occasion and has said that they would fulfil their share of the contract, the terms of which they and the federal government apparently have already agreed on. They have risen to the occasion and are prepared to go ahead.
I understand that in the estimates this year there is only the amount of $1 million. A million dollars will not go very far. I remember a speech made by the minister. I have referred to it before, and I have been corrected once or twice by the minister because I have quoted him as saying in my presence, because I listened to him that night in the technical school at Saskatoon, that it was a $110 million project, and apparently the money was going to be provided for the project by the dominion government. That was previous to the election of 1945. I must say in all honesty that the minister corrected me and said that at least some of those millions he had mentioned would be spent on the St. Mary scheme in Alberta; but whatever it is, I should like to see some of it spent on actual work which would produce not reports of engineers and technicians but some water upon the lands of Saskatchewan. There is of course now- I shall not use the word "excuse"-the reason that we are faced with defence expenditures which might preclude this sort of thing; but as I have said, progress must go on. We are not going to get out of these defence expenditures in the next three months, three years or ten years. In the meantime do hon. members not think that one of the best defences

against anything which might happen is to make this country strong internally so that it might have food with which it might supply its own homes and the homes of its allies in other parts of the world?
I shall leave it at that, sir, with the plea that the minister and hon. members will all work to the end that that scheme so long planned, so long projected, so long a reason for hope on the part of the people of the western plains, will finally and soon be fulfilled.

Mr. Chairman, I should like on this occasion to say what has been in my mind for a long time. Some years ago at a municipal convention in Saskatoon I delivered a speech concerning the South Saskatchewan river project, and I should like to discuss the subject at greater length on this occasion.
In doing so may I direct the attention of hon. members to some facts. In Canada we have witnessed a concentration of what we have described as defence measures. People have been brought to the point where they think that defence is the only matter of importance. We have listened to speeches from hon. members on both sides of the house who have referred to economies that could be made, and it has been said that for the sake of defence every possible economy must be carried out.
My personal view is that in establishing this standard public thinking has gone a little too far. We realize that it is right and proper to defend our country, and that it is right and proper to have our people believe that they must sacrifice for the good of all. But it must be clearly understood that we cannot economize in agriculture, because to do so would be to economize on the very thing that will make our country strong.
There was an old saying that the army travels on its stomach, and I suggest that, whether it be in the east or in the west, the manufacturing industry is in the same position. The man who produces in eastern Canada travels on his stomach. Those of us in western Canada are not asking to have anything to do with war contracts. It is understood that we have out there a climate entirely satisfactory for flying. We enjoy many hours of daylight and of sunshine, which have enabled the Department of National Defence to establish airfields in western Canada. While I am not entirely satisfied with the location of those airfields, I am satisfied to have them in western Canada. That is our contribution, and that is what Canada is doing to reward us for our loss of war contracts.
The development on the South Saskatchewan river depends on the view taken of that

project by people in eastern Canada. We need money from the east to develop what we have in the west. I could talk for some considerable time about what I believe should be done in the far north. We have fought hard for a development in that area involving the area from Flin Flon up to Sherridon and Lynn Lake. The development in that area is just beginning.
To return to the development of the South Saskatchewan, I would point out that industry in eastern Canada enjoys protection, and that it supplies the west with goods. Between 1920 and 1948 we produced in western Canada over 12 billion bushels of wheat. Just think of that! We have sold that wheat on the markets of the world, and thus have given to the industries in eastern Canada a good standard of living.
Let me add that people in eastern Canada will not be hurt in any way by the development of the South Saskatchewan river. That dam will supply energy and water, and eventually will supply the people of eastern Canada with more money. It will not cost them anything, because it will pay for itself. All we are asking you to do is to develop this project, and to keep in mind what it will mean for the people of western Canada to have a lake about a hundred miles long. It makes very little difference, perhaps, to the people of the east, because they do not suffer from lack of water power. We have plenty of water, but it runs away, and we have no control over it. Our rains come at this time of the year, but the water flows away in torrents, down the Saskatchewan river, out into lake Winnipeg, up through the Nelson and out into Hudson bay. That water is lost.
All we ask is a chance to save it, to control it and to see if we cannot develop something worth while in that dry area. If that is done I am satisfied that we will have the benefits of cheap power, as it is enjoyed in eastern Canada. Out west it must be developed at the present time from coal and steam, and it becomes very costly. In my town it is generated by a diesel engine. I wonder if hon. members have any idea what the cost is. I will tell them that for light and power I pay twenty-seven cents per kilowatt.
We cannot continue on that basis. If it were not for the extra hours the farmers work we could not afford electricity. However, that is not the subject before us at the moment. I am trying to tell the people of eastern Canada we are not asking them to give us anything: we are asking them to put up the money and to begin work on the project, so that in future we can show that it has been worth while.

And it is worth while. I hope there is no one in the eastern part of Canada who will suggest that it is not worth while and should not be started. We need this development, and we enthusiastically support the control of that body of water. It is vital and necessary to Saskatchewan.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words at this time. I have listened with considerable interest to what has been said by some of my colleagues and I rise really to support the very sensible observations made by the hon. member for Kindersley. I do not want to enlarge on this at this time, but the South Saskatchewan river development is a very vital project. As far as the riding of Meadow Lake is concerned, the results will be indirect as I am in somewhat the same position as the hon. member for Peace River. I think the hon. member for Peace River should be commended for looking on this as a national project. I think that is about all that requires to be said with regard to the South Saskatchewan development. It will benefit all of the province of Saskatchewan.
All of Canada.

That is just what I was going to say. Anything that benefits the province of Saskatchewan is going to add to the economy of the whole nation. I was interested in what the hon. member for Lake Centre said with regard to reopening negotiations under the world wheat agreement. I come from a wheat growing area and I am just as much interested in increased returns for the wheat farmer as anyone else. However, I think a matter of this kind should be gone into with some caution because when you reopen an agreement for re-negotiation it can be revised two ways, upward or downward.
Canada is not in a very commanding position as far as the revising of the world wheat agreement is concerned. On the average we have 200 million to 250 million bushels of wheat to dispose of annually on the world market and as such we are not in position to set the price. Some years ago the United States used to sow about 56 million acres to wheat, but in recent years the average has been from 75 million to 79 million acres. Their farmers have found it profitable to continue that production and the result is that annually they have a surplus in the neighbourhood of 500 million bushels of wheat.
The United States is able to sell 80 per cent of its grain on the home market and can thus set a domestic price. That price is set higher than the world price with the result that the 500 million bushels or the 20 per cent surplus is pretty well paid for by their own economy

Supply-Agriculture
and costs them virtually nothing. When you have something that costs you virtually nothing you are able to put it on the market at a very low price if you so desire. With a surplus of that kind they are able to say what the world price should be.
I think they have set the price pretty well at $1.80 and they are the people who will likely set the price if the agreement is re-negotiated. I do not think there is much chance of the price being revised downward, but it is a possibility. We are just a minor stockholder in this company, as it were, because we contribute only a small portion of the wheat. As I say, the United States has 500 million bushels of an exportable surplus, with a domestic economy that consumes 80 per cent of the total production. That creates a situation where they can set a domestic price and pay for the 100 per cent out of the 80 per cent sold domestically. They are then able to dispose of the 20 per cent surplus pretty much as they see fit and at any price they wish.
I do not have anything against what the hon. member for Lake Centre said. If it could be arranged, I think it would be a good thing. But I think we should hold in the back of our minds the realization that we might run into some trouble if we insisted on re-negotiation. If anything along this line is done I think it would be best to first have some private talks with the United States to see what their opinion would be and if they might cause us any trouble we would be better off not to ask for any re-negotiation of this world wheat agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam and a few of the other problems facing agriculture today. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Meadow Lake and the hon. member for Mackenzie speak on this matter. Like myself, they represent constituencies which are not directly affected by the irrigation scheme on the South Saskatchewan river. We would benefit indirectly through the power development. My own constituency and that of Mackenzie would also benefit indirectly from the flood control that would result. In those two constituencies, as well as in Churchill constituency, there are large areas in the delta of the Saskatchewan and Carrot rivers which are flooded annually. If this flooding could be controlled, more land could be brought into 'cultivation for less money than we will have to spend on the South Saskatchewan river dam. The indirect benefits to agriculture in the central part of the province will be much greater probably than the benefits to the northeast section.

I had the opportunity last year to visit Idaho, Utah and Washington, returning home through Alberta. I was able to see many irrigation works in those areas and the changes brought about therefrom. The developments that have occurred in those areas as a result of irrigation are really astonishing. I am sure that every member from western Canada is one hundred per cent behind this development. I am sure also that the members from eastern Canada, realizing what it will mean to western Canada and indirectly to their own part of the country, will support this particular project.
We have talked about it for a long time. I know the Minister of Agriculture is behind it one hundred per cent. The difficulty seems to be to convince the treasury board and to get the necessary funds voted for the development. To many of us from western Canada it seems that it is easier to have money voted for projects in the east than it is to get the treasury board to pass similar votes that affect western Canada. That should be overcome. I am sure the eastern members will agree with us from western Canada that this development should be proceeded with at once, rather than two or five years from now. I understand from the report of the engineers that it will take at least seven years to complete this dam. It is to be a packed-earth dam which cannot be built in one or two years. It is a process that has to go on for from five to seven years before it can be completed. If we wait another two or three or four or five years before we start, that simply means it will be that much longer before we get any power. I believe $10 million is all that could be spent this year, and. I do not think that would be missed from our budget. I believe this is something to which the government should give consideration, something the whole house should support, and I would like to hear from some of the eastern members with respect to it. I know they have heard a great deal about our problems in western Canada; I know they have a great many problems of their own here in the east, but I am convinced that this project should be commenced at this time.
I was surprised at some of the statements by the hon. member for Meadow Lake as to the difficulty in arranging any discussion of the world wheat agreement. I believe his reasoning was a bit wrong. Among other things the hon. member said he thought the United States was responsible for setting the ceiling of $1.80. I do not believe the United States was at all responsible for setting that ceiling. That was a negotiated ceiling, and naturally the consuming countries rather

than the producing countries were anxious to keep it as low as possible. It was only after long negotiations that the final price for floors and ceilings was fixed under the agreement. The hon. member suggested that we were rather a small toad in the puddle. As a matter of fact that is not so; we deliver more wheat than any other country under that agreement. Anyone who has studied the agreement understands that 1,000 votes are given the consuming countries and 1,000 are given the producing countries. The number of votes given a country is based upon its deliveries under the agreement, or in the case of the consuming countries upon the amount bought by them. Of the 1,000 votes given the producing countries Canada has 445, so it will be seen that we represent the largest single block of votes among the producers.
I believe this matter should be given serious consideration at this time. As a matter of fact I believe the wheat board should be placed under the Department of Agriculture. It is now many years since wheat was placed under the Department of Trade and Commerce. At that time wheat was probably our most important exportable product; certainly it was a very important item in our export trade. It is still an important item, but it does not have the significance it had at that time. Today our exports of wood products, pulp and paper, minerals and so on have greatly increased, so wheat does not have the same importance in our external trade that it had when it was placed under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Today the wheat board handles not only wheat but coarse grains as well. In those coarse grains they handle the product which eventually determines the production of dairy and meat products in Canada, since that production cannot take place unless you first produce the coarse grains which enter into those commodities. It seems to me that if the Department of Agriculture is to have the control it should have over our agricultural industry so we can have a balanced agricultural program for Canada, the department should have control of the marketing of wheat and coarse grains.
Earlier this session I suggested that the wheat board should be enlarged. Two years ago we passed an amendment to the wheat board act which would permit the appointment of two additional members, making a board of five. When I mentioned the matter earlier this session the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated he was prepared to appoint additional members if he could find suitable men who would work harmoniously with those already on the board and who had the 80709-228

ability to do the job that would be expected of them. The minister asked if I could suggest any men who would be suitable for these positions. Well, it is not my place to make such suggestions, but since that time I have consulted several farm organizations who have told me they know of men who would be suitable for appointment, so I think the number of members of the board should be increased. In appointing new members I believe two points should be taken into consideration. In the three present members of the board we have men who thoroughly understand the selling of our grain. That has been their business; they have been at it for twenty-five or thirty years; they have come up through the various grain organizations, and they understand that part of the board's work. But in the handling and selling of coarse grains it seems to me we should have on the board someone who has a broader view of the whole agricultural industry of this country. I would suggest that in making these two additional appointments one man at least should be a livestock producer from western Canada or a man from one of our western universities who understands the wider aspects of agriculture rather than just the selling of our grains. In the other appointment I think we would be well advised to consider someone from the east who understands the livestock situation and knows something about the distribution of feed grains in this part of the country. Then we as producers and sellers of grain in western Canada would have on the board a representative of those who consume the greater portion of our products, who would be able to give advice on the best methods of keeping our eastern markets. It seems to me that in this way we would have a more effective board and would be better able to handle our coarse grains.
Earlier this session I made a suggestion in reference to the handling of coarse grains, which at present are sold on the Winnipeg grain exchange to the extent of about 75 per cent of the total. I have the figures in a return of February 9, giving the number of bushels sold in that way. I have placed them on record before, so I need not repeat them today, but they show that 75 per cent of our coarse grains are sold through the grain exchange at the present time, with the other 25 per cent being sold by the board direct to the consumer. I am convinced that if we are to maintain our market for coarse grains in eastern Canada we must find some more direct method than selling through the Winnipeg grain exchange. I believe we should move our coarse grains to the east while they are still under the control of the wheat board, using government facilities in eastern Canada

Supply-Agriculture
for the storage of the grain and establishing direct sales agencies which would deal with the eastern consumers. It seems to me that is the only way we are going to be able to maintain and develop our market for coarse grains in eastern Canada, and for that reason I am convinced that we should have a representative from eastern Canada on the wheat board, together with another agricultural man who would understand -the relationship between the price of coarse grains and the price of livestock. In that way we could maintain a better balance and could get back into the production of livestock in both west and east.
If you are to build up a livestock industry, there must be a reasonable relationship between the price of coarse grains and the price of livestock. It seems to me that we need more co-operation between the east and the west, between the livestock producer and the grain man in Canada today, if we are to get back to a reasonably balanced type of agriculture. I am convinced that it could be done through our wheat board if we enlarged the number on that board to include representatives from other sections of agriculture than the producers and sellers of grain. I hope the minister will give some consideration to this matter of placing the wheat board under the control of the Department of Agriculture rather than the Department of Trade and Commerce.
For a great many years we did not have agricultural legislation in this country which permitted the producers to set up the necessary marketing boards to market their products. Under the British North America Act agriculture is in a dual position. It is partly under the control of the province, and partly under the control of the dominion. As a result of this there was a great deal of what army people term "passing the buck" so far as agricultural legislation was concerned. In the last fifteen years we have gotten away from that a bit, so that today we have on the statute books four major acts dealing with agriculture. First, there is the wheat board act, passed in 1935 by the Bennett government and since amended many times. It is doing a reasonably good job in the marketing of wheat. As I said, there are still some improvements that could be made to it.
The second major piece of legislation which we have concerning the marketing of agricultural products is the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939, and the Wheat Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939. Then we have the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944, and the Agricultural Products Marketing Act of 1949. Those are the four major acts dealing with agriculture which we now have. You will notice one

thing that is common to them all, and' that is that they were all passed in a year before an election. When they were passed many fine promises were made as to what their effect upon agriculture would be. Some of them have had the desired effect, and some have not.
The Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act passed in 1939 was an act for the marketing of agricultural products through co-operative organizations. Under that act the dominion government will guarantee an initial payment up to eighty per cent of the average price for the three years previous on a product which is being marketed by a co-operative organization. There have been quite a number of co-operative organizations selling agricultural products under that act. Since the act was put into force there has only been one occasion that I know of when the dominion government became liable for a payment under that guarantee. I believe in 1947 a guarantee was made to the silver fox producers in Canada, and there was a deficit under that operation. It seems that not only the co-operatives handling fox pelts were guaranteed, but a lot of other organizations were apparently able to come under the act. Even the Hudson's Bay Company was able to qualify for a payment of several thousand dollars on fox pelts marketed by the -company. I believe the original intention was that the act should deal only with co-operatives, but it was certainly extended on that occasion. The act is a good one. It permits orderly marketing by co-operative organizations by reason of the dominion government guaranteeing their bank loans for the initial payment up to eighty per cent of the average price over the past three years.
As a matter of fact, floor prices could be placed under agricultural products through the operation of this act. The act has never been used for that purpose. In no case of which I am aware-perhaps the Minister of Agriculture can correct me-has an initial payment been guaranteed up to eighty per cent of the average price for the last three years. As I say, there may be cases in which that has been done. I do not know whether the co-operatives have ever asked for a guarantee as high as that.

It is a matter of negotiation, and, as has been said, I do not believe there has been any case where the guarantee has been as high as eighty per cent. The act provides for eighty per cent, but it is usually around sixty per cent.

That was my understanding, that it was usually around sixty per cent.

The act could be used, however, if there was a disastrous drop in the price of any particular agricultural product which was being marketed by a co-operative, such as the alfalfa produced in northern Saskatchewan. I believe those producers are using this act since their incorporation.
The third act which was passed was the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944. When that act was passed it was to support agricultural prices during the transition from war to peace. As hon. members will recall, the act was renewed from year to year until last year it was made permanent legislation. Again this is a good act, but it has its limitations. When the minister introduced the act, he gave us to understand that it would be used to support agricultural prices at a level which would equal the cost of production in this country, plus a reasonable return for any sacrifices which the farmers had made during the first two or three years of war, during which time everyone recognized that agricultural prices were below the cost of production. Unfortunately that formula, if it was a formula, has not been used, and year after year agricultural organizations from eastern and western Canada have been asking the government to have some formula in the act which would indicate the floor to which the price for any agricultural product may fall. I believe the government should give consideration to placing some formula in the act.
Today we are operating alongside the United States, and this government has indicated that it believes our prices must be allowed to find their level somewhere near the level of prices in the United States. But we find that the farmers in the United States have floor prices under a great many of their products, in particular their major products. In the matter of wheat, for instance, the United States floor price is in the neighbourhood of $2 per bushel, and the price has been consistently above that. The Canadian floor price as announced by the minister, or the initial payment-I am not going to argue with the minister over terms- is today $1.40 for our coming crop. Now, that is a difference of 60 cents per bushel. Yet I believe our production costs in Canada are as high as the production costs in the United States, with the exception of the cost of land. So far as farm machinery and other production costs are concerned our costs are as high, and yet we find our floor price is 60 cents below the floor price in the United States.
It is the same with many other agricultural products. If we are to have legislation which is to be effective, which is to mean 80709-228J
