anything to our industry in this country, I think we should have a formula under our Agricultural Prices Support Act so that agriculture in this country would feel secure in going ahead and expanding production. To my mind that is the main reason why we are not getting the expanded production that we might expect in meat products at this time when prices are high. I believe that the main factor is the fact that the average farmer does not feel secure in starting in to* build up a herd, at present prices. Unless he has some guarantee in the form of some formula in our price support legislation,, which will justify him in going ahead and expanding his production, I am afraid we shall continue to produce at the level at. which we are now producing, and probably at an even lower level than we have at the present time. Under present conditions large shipments of our breeding stock are going to the United States. That situation will continue, and we shall find our herds decreasing in this country unless there is some security, some guarantee to the producer that if he goes into production he can expect these prices to be reasonable over a period of years.
The other piece of legislation which we have on our statute books is the Agricultural Products Marketing Act which we passed in
1949.	Here again we have a good piece of legislation if it has authority and if it will do the things which the Minister of Agriculture indicated to the house might be accomplished under it when the act was passed.
Hon. members will recall that back in 1934 we had an agricultural products marketing: act passed by the Bennett government at that time but which was found to be ultra vires and was discarded. This time we have started from a different angle; and the minister indicated to the house that, having obtained the view of the law officers of the crown, he believed our present act would do for us the job that it is supposed to do. There is, however, still a great deal of doubt with regard to the legality of the act if it is, extended to set up central selling agencies wherein two or more provinces will get together to market their products in inters provincial and export trade. I do not suppose that we shall know definitely whether that act is legal or not until an actual case* has been tried. But we have never had from; the government any assurance that I know of to the effect that if such action is taken to prove the act to be ultra vires, if and when it is operated by two or more provinces, the government will see that the act is amended or that the necessary amendments are made

to our- constitution in order to make the act do the job that it was intended to do; and until the government will come forward and give some definite assurance that it is their intention to stand behind this act and that, if it is not legal in its present form-if central selling agencies are set up by various provinces in order to market their products in interprovincial and export trade, and if a test case is taken and it is found that the act is not legal-that it will stand behind the organizations and see that the necessary amendments are made to the act or that the necessary amendments are made to our constitution to see that the act is operative.
These are a few of the things that are facing our agricultural producers today. Various members who have spoken have indicated that the agricultural income during the last year has fallen in Canada by something over $200 million. In the province of Saskatchewan alone-owing, as other hon. members have stated, partly to weather conditions and partly to the fact that our crop was not all marketed last year-the drop in income this year has been approximately [DOT] $160 million. On the other side of the picture the increase in our cost of production has been approximately $50 million in that province; it is more than that across the dominion. Those are serious problems for the man who is doing the work and producing the food. I feel that some consideration should be given to them and that certain amendments to this legislation which I have indicated should be brought before this house either at this session of parliament or at the next one.

Mr. Chairman, I agree one hundred per cent with the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Some of the members from the west say that they cannot sell the South Saskatchewan river project to the eastern members and to treasury board. I have been in this house for eleven years and I have never heard a member from eastern Canada oppose any irrigation project for western Canada. I think that any worthwhile legislation will be supported by members from eastern Canada.
I should like to get out of the west for a few minutes and get down to a section that is farther east than the one which hon. members have been talking about, namely the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Potatoes.

I consider that we have not received fair treatment in the maritime provinces. I know that we have not received fair treatment in regard to the production of potatoes in the two provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We have a

plan down there. We have had one for the last two months. It is working out and giving good results. But the farmers down there who are now planting the crop, or have practically finished doing so, do not know what is going to come out of that plan. They know that some arrangement was made by the New Brunswick and the Prince Edward Island marketing boards with the Department of Agriculture in the two provinces and the department at Ottawa whereby an arrangement was made under the co-operative marketing act of 1939. I understand that a producer's initial payment of $1.20 per barrel or 44 cents a bushel was set up. But I have never been able to find out whether or not that is correct. What I should like to know is this with regard to the potato growers of those two provinces who sold their potatoes last fall at the ridiculously low price of 60 cents a barrel, the farmers that were forced to sell. They were mainly veterans who returned from the war and took up farms under the Veterans Land Act and who could not hold their potatoes until spring, or until the last two months. I should like to know whether they are going to receive an initial payment of $1.20 a barrel. That is what I should like the minister to tell the house when he makes his statement.
I should like to see fair treatment clear across Canada for the primary producers of Canada. I will favour that as long as I am in the house. I should like to see fair treatment for all farmers. The United States have given great support prices for agriculture. I think they went too far in the United States. However, when in 1949 they paid out sums such as $822 million for cotton, $767 million for corn, $750 million for wheat, $241 million for flaxseed and linseed and $170 million for peanuts, I think they went too far in the United States. We received no such treatment in Canada. When the prices support act was introduced in 1944 we expected to get fair treatment. I do not think that act has been enforced as the minister explained to us it would be when he introduced it in parliament. I am sure we have not had fair support under it.
I understand that the minister hopes to have the crop of potatoes in the two maritime provinces which is now being planted under the co-operative marketing act. I understand that a plan is to be worked out with the marketing boards of the two provinces to deal with the crop now being planted. A few weeks ago the minister told me that he hoped to have this done. I understand that under the present act the initial payment has to be set in the spring of the year when the crop is planted. It is similar to the way wheat is dealt with. The initial price for

wheat grown in western Canada was announced in this house a few weeks ago. I have heard nothing about potatoes since the starch program was set up some time ago. I believe that some potatoes were shipped apart from the starch program, I suppose under the co-operative marketing act. When the minister speaks I want him to tell the house just where we in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island stand in regard to the 1950 and 1951 crop of potatoes.
What about the rest of Canada?

You look after yourselves. All that I have heard in the eleven years that I have been here is about western Canada, and that is all I have heard since this item came up. If you cannot talk of wheat you talk of water:	You must have
more than water out there. What we want is fair treatment.
That is all we are looking for.

We are willing to support the west in getting fair treatment. Fair treatment should be given to every primary producer, because if you force the farmers off the farms-and they have been going off the farms by hundreds weekly down in the maritime provinces and coming to Ontario and Quebec-I do not know what you are going to do for food, because food does not come out of the kitchen. It is not manufactured in the kitchen. I takes a lot of work to produce food. If you are going to bring all the farmers off the farms and into the factories of the two central provinces, I do not know where you are going to get your food.
The plan which has been in effect in the last two months has been a wonderful help to the two maritime provinces. The price of $1.20 a barrel in New Brunswick and 44 cents a bushel in Prince Edward Island does not give them the cost of production. However, it is better than the price of 60 cents a barrel and 20 cents a bushel, and they are thankful for it. But I should like to see some help given to the farmers who were forced to sell their potatoes for practically nothing last fall. They should have the same price as the grower who is able to hold his potatoes until spring. These people were not able to hold their potatoes. They had not the storage; they had not the finances to hold their potatoes until spring. Therefore they had to sell them for very much less than the cost of production. I hope the minister will make a statement on this matter and tell us where we stand in these two provinces.

I want to thank the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton who has just taken his
Supply-Agriculture
seat for the co-operation he has offered on behalf of the eastern members when we come here seeking a square deal for our own farmers all across Canada.
I feel that the farming industry has been neglected far too much in the past. The importance of this industry is not recognized by those in office. Until that is done we will not have a prosperous Canada, which it is possible to have if proper policies are pursued.
I am sorry to see at this time that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have been slashed by something like 35 per cent. In my opinion that is not good business at this time. We have been told that we must devote all our energies to defence, but I think we should also point out that the people of this country, and the people in other countries with whom we are allied, must have food, and lots of it. speechtext:
The government of the
United Kingdom has today issued the following announcement, but with the restriction that it is not to appear in the newspapers until tomorrow morning. Those newspapers will be published within a few hours after the time I make the announcement here. The announcement is as follows:
It has been agreed to hold a conference of defence ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and Southern Rhodesia. The ministers have decided that London will be a convenient meeting place and the conference will open there on June 21. It will consider certain defence problems arising in regions of common concern to these countries including the Middle East and also consequential questions of equipment and training which are of mutual interest to them. Canada will be represented at the conference by an observer.
That is the end of the announcement to be made in London. The desirability of holding such a conference was discussed on the occasion of the meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in London last January. It was then the feeling of the governments of the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Southern Rhodesia that it would be helpful to hold a conference of the defence ministers of those countries to
Defence Conference
consider problems arising in regions of special concern to them, including the Middle East.
Canada has, of course, special and direct defence responsibilities in the north Atlantic region. Our interests in the regional defence problems which will be under discussion at the forthcoming conference are less direct than those of the other commonwealth countries which will be represented there. The government has accordingly decided that it would be appropriate to be represented at the conference by a civilian and a military observer. Our position in this respect is fully appreciated by other commonwealth governments concerned.

The house resumed in committee of supply, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
1. Departmental administration, $336,942.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose before six o'clock I was pointing out the importance of agriculture to all Canadians, and was thanking the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton	for his
co-operation in seeing that agriculture got a square deal. I pointed out also that some members are giving practically all their support to the defence program, but without food the defence program would not be very far-reaching. For that reason I feel that agriculture is of great importance to this country. I was about to quote the figures in the estimates for agriculture for the fiscal year 1950-51 and for the present fiscal year. The agricultural estimates were $81,805,497 for the fiscal year 1950-51, whereas for the present fiscal year they amount to $53,131,838. There is a decrease of $28,673,659, or approximately thirty-five per cent. I am not feeling happy about this decrease in a department as important as agriculture.
During the afternoon we heard speakers from the various parties deal with the question of irrigation. Many good recommendations were made, to which I want to add my support. I do not feel it is necessary to reply to the different arguments, but even though the irrigation projects are not in my constituency I feel that they are of interest to Canada as a whole. Realizing that we cannot deal with our own particular district, I feel we should give all support to these programs because they are of benefit to the country as a whole. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River. On another occasion, I believe May 1, he gave

Supply

Agriculture
same particulars as to the effect of this act on farmers in his part of the country. The minister could see some flaws in this legislation, and brought in amendments to remove certain injustices. While I was a member of the agricultural committee which dealt with those amendments, I did not foresee the difficulties which exist in the Peace River district now. I do not believe the Minister of Agriculture foresaw them either, because whenever flaws in the legislation were pointed out to him he did not waste time in having them remedied. The particular reason for bringing in the amendments at that time was to prevent settling on marginal land. I feel that there is a new problem in the Peace River country, but I have no doubt that the minister will give further consideration to it before this session is completed, and bring in the necessary amendments to rectify the injustices which exist in that section of the country. This act is man-made, and I do not see any reason why we cannot pass some amendments to make it more effective in the interests of agriculture in all parts of the country.
The question of the international wheat agreement has also been dealt with. We find quite a lot of dissatisfaction throughout the country, particularly in the western provinces, because the Ontario wheat growers did not come under the international wheat agreement. There have been quite a few complaints around my part of the country about that, but I am not going to discuss it because the Ontario farmers grow a different grade of wheat which is useful for different purposes. So far as the international wheat agreement affects us, I feel that there are injustices in that agreement that should be rectified. It is not my intention to go into it in detail, but I feel that, if the recommendation of the hon. member for Acadia had been implemented at the time this agreement was first discussed in the house, we would not have had the present injustices. I expect many people are not aware that class II wheat is now being sold by the wheat board for nearly 40 cents per bushel more than the wheat that is being delivered under the international wheat agreement. I feel that that loss, in addition to the many million dollars that have been lost under another agreement just concluded, is a little too much for the prairie wheat growers to take without complaint.
The suggestion made by the member for Acadia was to the effect that the price of wheat should be tied to the price of other commodities in the countries where our wheat was sold. When the prices of other commodities went up or down, then the price of wheat would follow. This provision would 
give everyone a square deal, and that is all we are requesting for our farmers both east and west. As the agreement stands now, provision is made for a decrease of ten cents per bushel per year without any consideration whatever being given to the rapidly rising cost of production. But as matters stand at the present time, it looks as though the costs are going to increase while the price of our product will decrease as time goes on. As I have stated already, we are losing close to 40 cents a bushel on every bushel sold under the international wheat agreement at the present time, as compared with the price of class II wheat. That is too much for the farmers to be asked to lose. No compensation whatever, of course, is provided for. In spite of the champions of the grain exchange inside and outside the house, I am still firmly convinced that the wheat board system of marketing our grain is the one and only system that will give the farmers anything like a square deal. We had experience with the grain exchange many years ago; and if it is a good system for the sale of our wheat and other grains, why do not manufacturers and other producers take advantage of that system? Perhaps you would have the price of cars, lumber and household goods away down in line with agricultural prices today. If that were the case, I do not think you would have much complaint coming from the farmers of this country.
We find that some people who should know better-including some of the great self styled champions of the west who came here on the strength of the farmers' vote-even at the present time are going out and preaching against the wheat board, against international agreements and in favour of the Winnipeg grain exchange which has been rightfully described as one of the legalized gambling dens of the country. I am just as firm in my opinion today as: I have ever been that the gambling den should be put out of existence.
Earlier this session I suggested that the marketing of our grain should be taken out of the Department of Trade and Commerce and placed under the Department of Agriculture. I admit immediately that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is an extremely efficient man in his own line. But when you put him in a wheat field or a potato patch. I think he is entirely out of place. Perhaps the settlement of that agreement just about a year ago now is some of the best evidence we can get to back up the statement I have just made. The Minister of Agriculture has farmed, has. worked among farmers and knows his department and the intricacies of production and marketing as well as, or perhaps better than, most other hon. members

of the House of Commons. I think that the growers of grain and other products should have the advantage of the experience of the Minister of Agriculture.
We are devoting a great deal of our time and outr money to producing more and better food. But if government policy and government administration is going to give that food away without proper compensation to the farmer, why should the farmer continue to boost his production and improve the grade of the things he is producing? Even at the present time, while many hon. members are still commenting on the alleged raid made on the treasury by the farmers of the prairie provinces, we must realize that the consumers all over Canada-including the members of the House of Commons-are eating bread that is subsidized by the wheat growers of the prairie provinces to the extent of almost 40 cents a bushel. While many of them are well fed on that subsidized bread, we still have them coming here and1 complaining about the alleged raid made on the federal treasury by the farmers. But even after that crumb that fell from the rich man's table was paid to the farmer, let it not be forgotten that over a four-year period:, from 1945 to 1949, the wheat growers are still in the red to the extent of approximately $450 million on that deal, taking in the British wheat agreement and the subsidizing of the Canadian consumers. I therefore feel that a little bit more consideration should be given to our agricultural population.
In case there should be anyone who thinks we are being properly treated, I should like to ask this question and to receive an answer: Is there any other occupational group in this country which is treated in the same way. We do not have any cost plus system in figuring out the price of our farm produce; and when we come to examine the financial statement of many of our farmers, we do not have the large amounts that have been cited here in this chamber recently in connection with corporation profits.
We have been criticized here for rising and advocating a better deal for agriculture. In my opinion-and I believe the same opinion was expressed by the Minister of Agriculture some few years ago-we do not have nearly enough representatives of agriculture standing up for the rights of the farmer in the House of Commons. On this occasion when agriculture is being discussed, I should like to see members from the Atlantic to the Pacific stand up for the rights of the farmer; because when you have a prosperous agriculture, then you have guaranteed employment for labour, organized and unorganized, and for all other industries within the country. I feel that the time is long past 80709-229
Supply-Agriculture
when agriculture should have been brought up to the same level as other industries within the country. I believe the Prime Minister realizes the need for that step also because, speaking in southern Ontario only a couple of months ago, he raised that question; and it has been cited in the house here on one other occasion. I am not going to deal with it further tonight.
When it comes to fighting wars, where do you go to get your help for the factories? Where do you go to get your best fighting men in all services? You go to the farms of Canada. As proof that conditions on the farm are not what they should be, we find statistics showing that over 80,000 farm workers left the farm and moved to the city during the past calendar year. If that is not sufficient proof, then I think people ought to get around and see conditions as they are, not sit around here and listen to some of the old stories that have been told for years in connection with farmers and their business.
Since coming to the House of Commons I have been pleading, as my colleagues have been, for parity prices for agriculture. If we have that situation, I believe we shall have a much more prosperous, contented and united Canada than we have at the present time.

Before this item passes, Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to comment briefly on some remarks that have been made during this afternoon and evening with respect to the general condition of agriculture at this time. I believe that the farmers throughout Canada are looking to the government for action to enable them to lead a secure life, under conditions that will allow a reasonable standard of living. As has already been said a number of times today, the farmers are not asking for handouts. They are not asking for the highest prices the traffic will bear. What they ask for is some reasonable stability in their prices and in their costs of production.
So far as we in western Canada are concerned, in order to have a more stabilized agriculture one of our primary needs is to have a proper scheme of crop insurance. For that reason-we in the C.C.F. have always supported the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and we have always fought for its extension and its improvement at every opportunity. I must say that since this act was first passed in 1939 certain improvements have been made; but last year an amendment was brought down in this house which meant that farmers who once had received prairie farm assistance, and who once were eligible for it, were deprived of its benefits. I hope the time is not far distant, although I might

Supply-Agriculture
add there is no indication that it will be soon, when this government will take steps to increase the benefits payable under that act. The maximum benefits are $2.50 an acre on half of the cultivated acreage, and these benefits first applied under the original act over ten years ago. In spite of the fact that the costs of production have doubled or trebled since that time, there has been no upward revision of the benefits under the act. However, at times amendments have been brought in which have reduced the area in which the benefits might be paid until a far greater percentage of the farmers who do have a crop failure are eligible for the bonus.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River this afternoon. I agree with him that the amendments last year which have deprived certain farmers of the benefits of that act without any rhyme were a backward step and are working a hardship on a great many farms, particularly in Alberta. Although a great many of the farmers, because of that amendment, are not allowed to receive the benefits of the prairie farm assistance, nevertheless they are forced to pay into the fund one per cent, year in and year out.
When any person or any group of persons is obliged by law to pay premiums into a certain fund, they should not be deprived of benefits. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Peace River that last year in the agriculture committee I moved a motion asking that that backward step, which would deprive thousands of farmers of the bonus, be not taken. Even though I moved that motion I did not have the pleasure of the support, on the vote of the members in that committee, of the Social Credit party. I believe that the leader of the Social Credit group now believes that these amendments were unjust, and I am sure that the members of the agriculture committee from his group will agree with him, although, as I say, last year, when I attempted to take out of those amendments the retroactive feature, I was not fortunate enough to receive support from the members of the Social Credit group on the committee.
As I have said, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been of considerable benefit, but certain definite amendments should be made to that act, and should be made immediately. The maximum benefit of $500 now will buy only half or one-third the amount of goods that it would buy in 1939. The farmer who has two or three crop failures in a row, and is dependent upon- the $200, $300, $400 or $500 he receives from the Prairie Farm

Assistance Act, is certainly not going to be able to continue in the business of farming and maintain his family in decency. The amendments moved last year were absolutely unfair and uncalled for. They provided that, with certain exemptions, lands disposed of by His Majesty after the 31st day of December, 1940, would be no longer eligible for the bonus. As I said ini the committee at that time and in the house during the last session, I would have no objection at any time if the government would bring in amendments so that submarginal land properly defined would no longer be eligible for benefits provided that of course some other steps were taken to take care of the people who might be involved. But certainly arbitrary amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, such as we had last year, depriving people of benefits that they had enjoyed for over ten years, while forcing them to pay a premium into that fund year in and year out, are grossly unfair and should be corrected at an early date.
I agree with those who this afternoon pressed upon the government the need for doing something to revise the present ceiling prices in the international wheat agreement. I might say that I believe I was the first member who raised the question in the house, when on May 16 I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he would not consider getting in touch with the other nations signing the agreement to see if an upward revision of prices might not be negotiated. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce threw up his hands and suggested that he was not going to scuttle the agreement, inferring that 1 was suggesting that such a thing should be done. Mr. Chairman, there was no such suggestion from me or from anyone else that Canada should in any way abrogate the present international wheat agreement.
The only suggestion that we made was that in view of the terrific increase in the cost of production, our government, on behalf of the farmers, should suggest to the other signatories to that agreement that some upward revision in the ceiling price should be made.
It has been suggested in this house that Canada is a pretty unimportant member of the international wheat agreement, but I would point out that of the 1,000 votes held by exporting countries under that agreement Canada -holds 445. We certainly are an important country in that agreement, second in the exporting field only to the United States. Our quota is some 221 million bushels; the United States quota is 248 million bushels.

As has already been said, the United States government is subsidizing every bushel of United States wheat that is sold under the international wheat agreement. The United Grain Growers estimate that the subsidy the United States is paying will cost approximately $100 million. I am sure their government would be happy to take any practicable steps which might result in an upward revision of the ceilings, and consequently a reduction of the subsidy that the United States government is now paying. I want to point out, too-I do not think this can be pointed out too strongly-that the United States government subsidy on wheat being sold under the international wheat agreement has resulted in a satisfactory price for wheat to the United States farmer. The American public is paying as much for its wheat as any other country in the world, including even those countries outside the international wheat agreement. But the situation in Canada is entirely different.
Not only will this government not guarantee the farmers of Canada a parity price, but they are disposing of Canadian farmers' wheat to Canadian consumers at 38 cents a bushel less than class II wheat.
I suggest the government should establish a parity price for wheat, and parity prices for other farm commodities. They should be prices bearing a fair relationship to farmers' production costs. The farmer is not asking for a handout; but when the government sets the floor price for the coming crop at a figure as low as $1.40 a bushel, and forces the Canadian farmer to subsidize the Canadian consumer to the extent of 38 cents a bushel, then in my opinion the government is not playing fair with the farmers of Canada.
True, we have certain floor-price measures, but they are almost depression floor prices- 28 cents a pound on cheese, 58 cents on butter, $32.50 per hundredweight on hogs, 38 cents a dozen on eggs. In my opinion all those floors are far below the cost of production. When the producers of Canada see that floor prices are so low, naturally they reduce production. And when they reduce production, then of course there is a shortage of those commodities, with the result that prices to the consumers become high.
Our farmers are prepared to produce in abundance all these various agricultural commodities; but they ask that the government will guarantee to them reasonable floor prices based upon parity, which shall have some relation to their cost of production.

Irrigation out there does not mean just irrigation farming; it means the production of feed and fodder on irrigated land for the stabilization of a large area of agricultural land surrounding the irrigated parts.
Anything the government can do to provide the farmers in that part of Saskatchewan with twenty or thirty acres of irrigated land will certainly go a long way toward providing agricultural stability. I think what hon. members are interested in is what the government actually intends to do. If the government announced that it was going ahead with the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam I believe it would receive unanimous approval of the project from all sides of the house. I do not know of one group in the house that has opposed this suggestion. I believe that irrespective of which part of Canada we represent, we are all good Canadians and at all times we will consider favourably legislation that will benefit any particular province. Mr. Chairman, I notice that one of the members from Ontario has risen. This afternoon one question which was raised, and which I think probably I should say something about-it is not quite in the classification to which I have just referred- was that having to do with the marketing of potatoes. The matter was discussed by an hon. member from New Brunswick. Reference also was made to marketing plans being carried out in Prince Edward Island, as well as in New Brunswick.
It was suggested that the plan now in effect was organized under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939, and that is the case. I should say however that, when I made the statement which was referred to before the dinner hour to the effect that this plan should be applied in much the same way as some of the co-operative marketing plans have been applied to other products, the change in the procedure which was followed with regard to potatoes was not intended in any way to interfere with the procedure which would require to be followed if we were going to market the potato crop of the whole season.
As I stated on a previous occasion, those who represent the potato growers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island came here some little time ago and represented to us that there were 2,000 carloads of potatoes of top grade to be marketed. The hon. member, who gives us most information with regard to potatoes, stated on that occasion that he did not think I had set the figure sufficiently high. There has been some evidence since to indicate that probably he was right and that there were more potatoes than our officials had stated were to be marketed
'Mr. Argue.]
at that time in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Nevertheless the figures which I used on that occasion were presented to us by those who were asking for assistance, and that being the case I thought they would pretty well cover the quantity which would be marketed.
Two boards were set up, one in New Brunswick and one in Prince Edward Island, to deal with the potatoes in the two provinces. I suggested that they could best gain experience with which to set up similar organizations to market the coming year's crop if they made an attempt to market what was left of this year's crop under a plan of that kind. They accepted the advice and have carried out the plan of attempting to market the potatoes which were left.
We suggested to them that after discussion with the two plants which process potatoes into starch they said they would be prepared to pay 60 cents a barrel for potatoes to be utilized in the making of starch. I think it was agreed by all parties to the arrangement that 60 cents a barrel was not a sufficiently high price for grade A potatoes which could be used for table purposes, that table potatoes should bring a higher price than potatoes to be used in the making of starch. But in any case the highest price the starch producers thought they could pay for the potatoes was 60 cents, and they agreed to pay that. Therefore 60 cents was made the advance payment to the farmers on all potatoes delivered to the board.
It was understood that as large a percentage as possible of the potatoes would be sold for table use and it was hoped that they would bring at least $1.20. However, they would be sold for whatever price could be obtained on the market. After the results of the experiment had been obtained a full report would be made to the government as to what the returns had been for all the potatoes. We agreed that we would contribute something toward the pool that was set up that would make it possible for a further distribution to the producers. The maximum amount set was $300,000.
We have not yet had reports which make it possible for us to give consideration to what the payment ought to be and therefore I am not in a position to say what the final payment will be. We had a request by wire today from one province indicating that sales have been higher in quantity than were anticipated and they ask for a reconsideration of the amount which would be paid^ in, but the agreement up to the moment is" that up to $300,000 would be available to take care of providing a higher return at the end of the marketing of what was left of this year's crop.

That is applying tne principle of the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939 to the marketing of part of the season's crop.
Is $300,000 available to Prince Edward Island and a similar amount available to New Brunswick?

No; the total figure is
$300,000 to the two boards which are operating together on the plan.
Is no payment to be made for sales made in (the fall at very low prices?
There is nothing in the agreement that has anything to do with sales made before the agreement was signed. The agreement covers potatoes which had not been sold at the time it was signed.

It can be made to cover a whole season, but in this case it was not.
It should.

If it is indicated by those
who are operating the board and by those who produce potatoes that this is a suitable plan to apply to 1951, then an agreement will be made in advance and they will go on from there to market. I wanted to say something in regard to the reference this afternoon by the hon. member 
for Lake Centre-I am sorry he is not here at the moment-to the reports that have been put out toy the 'bureau of statistics with regard to farm income. These reports are given to the press in the form I hold in my hand. If you read the press reports carefully you will find that they say what is in this report I have, but I have not heard anyone who has discussed the matter in this house discuss what is in this report. This is a very full report on farm income for 1950 as compared with 1949, and here is what it says in regard to the question that has been quite fully discussed this afternoon and at other times:
The decline in the 1950 farm cash income is largely attributable to a drop in the cash receipts from the sale of grains and substantially smaller grain equalization and adjustment payments. While nearly $50 million were paid to prairie farmers in the form of participation and equalization payments during the past year, approximately $220 million were disbursed in 1949.
Now, the $220 million is just the amount which it was stated in the press the farmers' income was down in 1950 as compared with 1949. It says it was down because these participation payments had been made in the previous years.
A lowering of the initial price to producers and a poor quality crop combined to offset increased marketings during 1950 and to give a cash income from the sale of wheat of $380 million, almost 20 per cent below the returns realized in 1949. Commencing August 1, 1950, the initial price to producers on No. 1 northern wheat in store at the lakehead was lowered from $1.75 to $1.40 per bushel. Severe frosts in the prairie provinces during August caused! considerable damage to the crop and sharply reduced! the average grade.
What has happened to that since that time? There has been another payment on the wheat. It is true that it was not made before the first of January, but there has been another payment on the wheat of 20 cents per bushel. Then, in addition to that, there has been the payment on the oats, and the payment on the barley, that was delivered prior to January 1, 1951. Although I do not want to start another debate on it, there was another $65 million which was paid on some of the crops of the past. If you take all those figures, put them together and apply them on the payments made on the crops of 1950- which will eventually be done when those amounts are adjusted-you will find there is very little difference between the income for 1949 and 1950.
You will find a difference between 1949 and 1951 if you are going to keep that up.

My hon. friend has been dreaming that for the last fifteen years, and he has always been wrong. He has always been one year ahead of the actual statistics

in telling us that the farmers are going to suffer. His expenses have gone up.

His expenses have jumped some, yes, but his returns are just about the same. Certainly it is right. If they would stop there, it would not be so bad, but they do not stop there. Agriculture is the basic industry in this country-I think I had better agree that it is not always outside this house, either. Then, after saying agriculture is the basic industry in this country, they completely pass over the fact that up until recently wheat brought more new wealth into this country than any other product- gold, oil or anything else. You can raise more interest in this house by discussing gold or oil-
Or subsidies.

Yes, the subsidies to newspapers. You can raise more interest in this house discussing those items than you can by discussing wheat. When we discuss wheat members are inclined to say, "Oh, well, this is a day off for us." That is not very far from the truth, as most members in this house will agree. Let me repeat that more new money has come into this country from outside of it-if one were to take the last ten years one could say more than from any other source-in order to repay those of us who are producing surpluses to send out to get the wherewithal to buy the products of other countries. I believe we ought to emphasize that, and keep it before the people who are constantly referring to the wheat grower

I should refer to something else that was said this afternoon. I was going to correct it at the time, but I did not. Someone was arguing that the marketing of wheat ought to be administered by the Department of Agriculture. I might agree with that, but it is not. As a matter of fact, it has not been. The thing that I object to in what was said this afternoon is that it was put in the Department of Trade and Commerce because of its great importance at the time it was put there. Now they should give the small man the wheat.

That might help; and it
has remained in the Department of Trade and Commerce ever since. On the last occasion when the matter was discussed here I recall the then acting leader of the opposition stating when I had made the remark that two heads were better than one, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I agree very well-when we both offered opinions on a matter, it went along very well- the then leader of the opposition suggested that would be all right if either one of them were a real head. My remark at the time was that there was only one political party in Canada at that time that did not have a real head. I am not going to say that tonight because we have a leader in the house leading that party. I am going to say that we should realize the importance of wheat in creating a sound economic position in the Dominion of Canada.
Now, that brings me to the discussion of a question that was raised this afternoon, and that is the international wheat agreement. Over the years, in spite of what we have been thinking and saying in recent years, wheat has been dealt with under

different governments and in different ways. I have in my hand the London wheat agreement of 1933. It is sometimes suggested that wheat agreements are a product of socialism in Britain; at other times it is suggested that wheat agreements are a product of the minds of this government; and at still other times it is suggested that they are the product of the thinking of farm organizations.
The first international wheat agreement that we ever had was set up in 1933. When I look back to see who were the gentlemen who were there from Canada to set it up, I find that one was the then prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. He was the chairman of the committee that met in London in order to set it up. I find that another was the Hon. M. A. MacPherson, provincial treasurer of the province of Saskatchewan; and the third was Mr. Norman A. Robertson of the Department of External Affairs, who is still with us.
Those three men went to London to attend a meeting which made an agreement which came to be known as the London agreement, under which the wheat of the world was to be marketed through an international board. That agreement was signed by the government of the day and agreed to. The only reason it did not function was that the government of the Argentine broke the agreement later and it did not go into effect. But we set up in Canada four different organizations to operate under this agreement. One was set up here at Ottawa and one was set up in each of the three prairie provinces. Legislation was brought into the house in each of the three prairie provinces to set up the machinery to provide for the operation of those boards. I am not going into the detail in connection with it. I am only giving the history because of something that I read today in the Searle letter which is being quoted largely in the discussions in connection with this question. In that letter they say this, quoting from Patrick Henry:
I have but one lamp by which my feet are guided; and that is the lamp of experience. I know of no way of judging the future but by the past.
Then they go on to suggest that we should not judge the future by the past, and that we should not even judge the present by the past. Everyone in this committee knows that under the operations of the grain exchange, which is sometimes called the free marketing of grain, we never received, over a five-year period, a dollar a bushel for our wheat; never at any time under that system did we receive a dollar a bushel for our wheat over a five-year period. The only times that we have ever gone over $1.50 a bushel for our wheat were under

boards set up by governments which operated for the purpose of getting every cent they could for the farmers.
It is obvious that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, the leader of the government back in 1933, was convinced that that was the proper way to have the wheat marketed. It is true that we did not always agree with his methods of applying boards; but I recall that on the first occasion that I ever discussed board marketing of wheat, I discussed it on a platform in Calgary when the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was the other speaker; we were both supporting the pooling of wheat. That was before he became prime minister of Canada and before I was a member of the government of Canada or had anything to do with it. We were there as western public men, speaking on the platform in Calgary; he was a supporter of the board method of marketing wheat and so was I. I say that tonight in order to point up my suggestion that we should be extremely careful in the criticisms that we make.
Nearly everyone who has risen on the other side of the house has stated that we ought to do something about the international wheat agreement. I have the international wheat agreement here in my hand; and in spite of what has been said, I cannot find anything in it which gives any government the right to change the price of wheat or even to suggest that the price of wheat ought to be changed, under this agreement, inside the four years. The section which was read this afternoon, and which has been read on other occasions, is on page 24, and numbered 5. It is under article VI. Article VI sets out, in subsection 1, the maximum and the floor prices of wheat. Then it goes on, under subsections 2, 3 and 4, to deal with the methods by which you are going to adjust the payments in different countries and under different facts that may arise in connection with the value of currency, in order to meet the situation. Subsection 5 states as follows:
If any exporting or importing country represents to the executive committee that any price equivalent established under paragraph 2, 3 or 4-
It does not say "under paragraph 1".
-of this article is, in the light of current transportation or exchange rates or market premiums or discounts, no longer fair, the executive committee shall consider the matter and may, in consultation with the advisory committee on price equivalents, make such adjustment as it considers advisable.
I again submit that that does not say it was anticipated at the time this agreement was made that somebody was going to come along in two years' time and suggest that it ought to be changed. I can scarcely understand how persons who advocate the bulk

system of marketing as against the open-market system, can suggest that you make an agreement to last for two years, three years or four years and then that you come along in the middle of the agreement and say: Now we are going to change that. In other words, you have not a long-term agreement at all.
If I understand the views of the farm movement, and more particularly that part of the farm movement that is associated with the marketing of grain, the situation is that they believe first in the wheat board method of marketing grain and they would apply it one hundred per cent to the marketing of all grains. They would apply it not only to wheat but to all other grains. That is their belief, whether we agree with them or not. Then when they pass that mark, they say: We are in favour of having an international agreement-and they have always fought for it-that covers a period of time. The period of time that they have insisted upon over the years was about five years. When this agreement was made it was for four years-and not for five. I venture to say that no matter what anyone thinks about it now, there was not anyone who really sat in on the drawing up of that agreement-and the leaders of the farm movement sat in on it; that is, all the leaders of the farm movement that are associated with the marketing of grain sat in on it-who expected that there was going to be a change within the four years.
May I ask the minister a question at this point?
Yes.
Did the leaders of the farm movement marketing grain have anything to say in connection with the price obtained under that agreement?

Well, they were there as
advisers. Now that you have asked me the question, I think they had just about as much to say as anybody had to say, excepting a very few. The people who always have the most to say about a thing of that kind are the people who have something to sell and the people who are paying for it. We do not have to look very far to find out who had the money on this occasion and who had the grain. It has been discussed tonight. It has been pointed out that under some changes that have been made in the agreement, which do not concern prices, the United States now delivers more wheat under this agreement than Canada, although when the agreement was drawn we were to deliver considerably more than the United States. But circumstances have developed since which have changed that.

Well, now, how did they arrive at $1.80 when the question was being discussed at the time the agreement was formed? The first suggestion was that the ceiling should be $1.50, and the floor should be $1, and that those prices should prevail over the five years. In the meantime parity in the United States rose to $2 for wheat. The United States government guarantees 90 per cent of parity and 90 per cent of $2 is 1.80. It was $1.99 last year.

It was $1.80 at the time they were discussing the question. The United States government agreed to a figure of $1.80. So far as we were concerned we said that since the United States which has the cash and a great deal of the wheat, and the British who are the buyers of most of the wheat, the largest block of it, at least, are in agreement, there is no reason why we should not sign too. We have gone along with the arrangement. Australia said the same thing. Every other signer of the contract said the same thing.
We are all in this together. If the suggestion made a few moments ago to the effect that the United States is ready to reconsider prices is correct, well, the United States will reconsider it, and I have no doubt that again most of us will go along. But to say to this government that it is in a position even to suggest, let alone demand, what ought to be done in connection with the matter is to take the wrong attitude with regard to it; and I do not think that the leaders of the farm movement who are interested in the marketing of wheat are taking that attitude. I wanted to say that because we ought to keep this thing moving along both east and west on the basis of the facts as they are, and not get into the position of shouting for something which may suit people other than those who are in agreement with the plan which is being followed.
