All I want to say with regard to that is I am still satisfied to go along with the people who a few years ago put forth the arguments and the facts which convinced both the larger political parties in this country that this type of marketing was a good thing for the farmers. If you go back far enough you will find that we were all opposed to it, but the farm movement eventually convinced us that they were right. I have had no reason for changing my opinion. I still think they were right, and so I believe that we ought to go along under this agreement, meeting the conditions which are written into the agreement to the end of the four years, and then if we think the agreement was not good enough, let us try another one which will be better. In the meantime I think the only way that we are going to justify this kind of trading is to carry out what is written into the agreement.
I wanted to say that because I did not want anyone to misunderstand the position 1 will be taking with the Minister of Trade and Commerce or anyone else. In fact I intend, when this matter is being discussed outside the house or in it, to put forth the arguments which have been put forth by the farm organizations from time to time. I believe they were right in the beginning. I believe they are still right, and I base my decisions upon this little piece that I read to the committee a few moments ago. Experience teaches me that we are right; and I think it is better to take a little less for the product when production is at the peak and get a little more for it when production is not at the peak, even though sometimes, if you take a short enough period to do your calculating, you may be a little down in returns as compared with others.

May I ask a question? The minister says that he agrees with the farm movement in regard to the international wheat agreement. Does he agree with them also on their stand that the domestic market should pay the class II price for wheat?

Well, that is another matter about which it is a little difficult to be too confident. After all, if one goes back to his own sound principles, no matter to which party he belongs, in connection with matters of that kind, I think he usually concludes that countries that do keep their costs of production at about the same level as other countries with which they are dealing are more likely to come out of the general run [Mr. Gardiner.l
of transactions in a sound position economically. I do not know whether it would be a good thing to raise the cost of living to all consumers in Canada any higher than the cost of living is in the countries to which we deliver wheat. It may not be a good thing for us in the long run. I would not give a snap judgment on this question yes or no.
The cost of bread is higher in this country than in most countries, because it is subsidized in most countries.

I have not time to go into that in detail tonight; it is really not on my agenda, in any case, and I am discussing it only because others have discussed it tonight, and I am discussing it because I come from the section of the country that is concerned with it, apart altogether from what department I am in.
I now come to the South Saskatchewan project. Discussions tonight have been very much in line with the discussions that have taken place on previous occasions with regard to this project. I agree with the statement that was made by the hon. member for Assiniboia a few moments ago that if you were to put the question to this house tonight, or I think on any other night, we perhaps could get a unanimous vote in favour of it; at least no one would get up and say that he was opposed to it. Again, if I may be pardoned, I might just suggest to the house that there was one previous occasion when that happened, but when it was all over there were many who did not agree. After all, a government is never excused for being wrong, no matter who supported it at the beginning.	And it is the government's
responsibility to be right. Some people say we were not right on another occasion, and that it cost the people something. I do not agree with them. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre looks a little mysterious, as though he does not understand. Well, I will make him understand: Everyone in this house agreed that it was a good thing to have a wheat agreement with Great Britain-when it was put through. But not everybody agreed when it was all over.
And the same thing can happen in connection with projects of this kind, and because there is not anyone here more responsible for anybody wanting the South Saskatchewan dam than I am, I want to be sure that I am right this time-even if some people thought 1 was wrong last time, when I did not think I was, and do not yet.
There is nothing particularly new about this project. It is quite old. I made a little review of the history of it in order to carry

out what is said in the Searle suggestion that experience is a good thing. I find it has been discussed since away back about 1856.

It was first discussed by men sent out from the old department of the interior, even before we had a dominion of Canada-or from what was the forerunner of the department of the interior. They were sent out to look over that section of the country.
But, coming down to a much later date than that, a geological survey of a possible dam site was made by John A. Allan, consulting geologist, and a report prepared on July 9, 1943. In this report Professor Allan says:
I was previously acquainted with this part of the South Saskatchewan valley when in 1918 I examined the geology along the valley between Empress and Saskatoon.
And that is the very area we are talking about. Empress is on the Saskatchewan-Alberta boundary, and Saskatoon is a few miles below the point we are proposing for this dam.
To come down to more modern times, as early as 1918, Professor Allan was asked to make a report. At that time natural resources were all in the federal government. And so it is evident that the federal government did have some ideas, even back there, that this might be a possibility.
Now, following that up, under P.F.R.A., we had Professor Allan appointed again, and then later on in 1947 we had another report on it which has been tabled in the house. Those reports are all favourable. I must say to the committee that all my reports to the government have been favourable, and they will continue to be favourable. I have reported to the government on each occasion we have obtained a report to the effect that in my opinion it would be a good thing to build this dam.
This year?

Three or four years ago- five years ago, for that matter-every time there has been a report. I think it would be a good thing to build this dam.
Now, I am not an engineer; but I think everybody understands that I think that putting a body of water anywhere in the prairie provinces is a good thing. The hon. member for Saskatoon made a remark this afternoon which I found difficulty in understanding. He said he did not know why we put the dam in Saskatoon, and he has suggested that it might have been as well without it.
Supply-Agriculture
Well, I will tell him this, that I think now that dam has been there about twelve or thirteen years-
If I might interrupt; the minister has misinterpreted my statement. I certainly did not mean it that way. I do not know what he understood.

That is the way it sounded. But if this does nothing more than give the hon. member an opportunity to correct it, I think he will be pleased after he has read Hansard. I say that because I do not know of anything that is a greater asset to the city of Saskatoon than the fact that they have that dam.
On the other hand there is another point involved in it. There is only one thing I find it difficult to settle in my own mind with regard to the South Saskatchewan dam; and I would not have been able to satisfy my own mind had it not been for the fact that we had the dam in Saskatoon. The last criticism I have heard about the South Saskatchewan dam was that the dam would fill up with silt. Well, I have said Yes, that it may fill up with silt, some time-but it will be a long time after we have gone.
What I wish to say about the Saskatoon dam is that it is only twelve feet high. I think at least as much water has been flowing over the Saskatoon dam every year as will ever go over the South Saskatchewan dam yearly. The same amount of sediment would be there as would be behind the bigger dam, and that silt has not filled up the area above the dam at Saskatoon. It still looks like a very nice lake, and if it does that with a 12-foot head of water over twelve or thirteen years, since the other dam will be 210 feet high I think it will take a lot of silt to fill up the 210-foot one if all the silt that comes down has not filled up the 12-foot one.
About 150 years.

Most of us will agree that it has done a good job if it stays there that long.
What about the lake itself? I am satisfied I cannot come before you at this time, or before any other body, and prove the case, if you check this dam on this project only from the point of view as to whether it will pay directly interest on the money that is invested in it. I do not think I could do it to the satisfaction of the members of the House of Commons.
Have not the engineers given a favourable report?

Well, they have given a favourable report. But a favourable report does not make that too sure. I think the best

Supply-Agriculture
answer I can give to the question which that raises is a statement which is made in the report we had when we built the St. Mary dam. This has to do with the Lethbridge-Northern irrigation plan which is just north of Lethbridge, and the one which most nearly agrees in all of the facts in relation to it with the areas that will be affected by the building of the other dam.
The experience with the area in connection with the Lethbridge-Northern is something like this: they sold debentures under a 1915 Alberta act, and those debentures were guaranteed by the government of Alberta. They found that the cost was about $57 an acre for putting in their irrigation system. They tried to operate on that basis and collect from the farmer. The provincial government has paid the cost to the farmer concerned down from $57 an acre to $17 an acre. In other words, they have provided $40 an acre out of the treasury of Alberta, as I understand it. The hon. member for Peace River will know about this, because he was connected with it at the time.
That is right.

They found it necessary to do that. I venture to say that men can get up in the house and prove that at least $25 million out of the $103 million would never be paid back to the government of Canada under any part of the scheme; and they might be able to prove that even $40 million might not be paid back. I am going to read what an independent investigator said about the northern Lethbridge project, and then I want you to ask me the question: Do you think it was worth while? Here is what was said:
In 1924, when the Lethbridge northern district was first irrigated there were only about 300 families in the area. Now about 900 families occupy farms on the project. Belts of fine trees shelter small fruits, flowers, and vegetables which grow in abundance. It is estimated that the project directly supports 10,000 people. A railway parallels a gravelled highway to Lethbridge and power lines bring the conveniences of the city to the farms. At Picture Butte, near the centre of the district, there is an up to date sugar factory, beautiful homes, trees and green boulevards. A few miles west of Picture Butte is Park lake now a provincial park, with ornamental and shade trees, a beach, dressing rooms, playground equipment, stoves, picnic tables, and benches. A few years ago all this was treeless, waterless, drought scorched prairie.
I do not think you could get a better description of a conversion of an uninhabitable area into one that is inhabited by people with a very considerable degree of comfort. I continue:
The social and community advantages resulting from irrigation deserve special emphasis though these benefits can only be partly indicated statistically. These advantages were observed by the committee on all projects visited and , a good

example is found in the Lethbridge northern irrigation district. Here an area of some 360 square miles, equivalent to ten townships, has been transformed in less than two decades from sparsely settled prairie subject to periodical crop failures and soil drifting to a thriving community of farm homes, towns and villages. During this period the number of farm holdings increased from 300 to over 900 and the population, rural and urban, increased from 1,500 to 10,000. As a result educational facilities have been greatly improved by the establishment of modern consolidated schools; electrical power has become available; a gravelled highway has been constructed through the project; a branch railway line constructed since the district was erected provides shipping facilities; and a park established in connection with a storage reservoir on the project provides recreational facilities for the surrounding area.
Again I repeat that the putting of a lake 135 miles long and 185 feet deep at the dam in the middle of the best farming section of the prairie provinces will do something which nature has done in other places. We all know that all nature has to do to create a lake is to leave a bar of rock across a stream. But nature did not do that here. However, all the facilities are there to do it. What we are asking the two governments to do is to provide the ways and means of putting that bar up which will in turn create a lake. With the lake there I am sure that in two decades you can do to that whole area what was done in two decades to the northern Lethbridge area.
Some hon. members are going up to Chalk River tomorrow. Some hon. members were with me when we went to Churchill. Other hon. members have been to other places. But if hon. members want to have their eyes opened as they have never been opened before, if they have never been out there, I suggest that they take a plane to Medicine Hat.
Hear, hear.
But do not stop in Medicine Hat.
Hear, hear.

Take a car out of Medicine Hat. If you let us know, I feel sure we can arrange to have the P.F.R.A. provide busses to drive you from Medicine Hat to Lethbridge any time around July 1 or the end of June. If you do that and you are not one hundred per cent an advocate of this plan after you come back, then I miss my guess.
While I have driven the road many times before, I drove it for the first time last year at that particular time of year. I decided to go to the stampede and I was accompanied by three . people. During the drive south from Medicine Hat they kept wondering for mile after mile why people stayed there.

Knowing what was ahead of the people who were staying there I did not say anything. About the middle of the afternoon we crossed a road allowance and then everyone in the car thought they were in another country. They felt sure it was not the same country they had been driving through. They were reminded of trips they had made to California and other places. The growth was what you would expect in semitropical areas. The difference between the two places was such that you could not understand why people were living under one set of conditions in one place and under another set of conditions right alongside.
I said to them that the reason those people had been staying there for twenty years was that they had been led to believe that somebody was going to put water on their land and make it look like the country we had entered. We have just completed the St. Mary river dam which will put water on that land. What we suggest now is that we should make the central part of Saskatchewan the same.
What does the government permit me to say to you tonight? They permit me to say this: They know I am convinced, they know the people out west are convinced, they think likely when we are all through that they are going to be convinced also, but they want to be sure that they are right when they make the decision to go full blast ahead. They asked me to do one thing more for them. I said, "What is the one thing more?" "There are one, two or three experts that we would like to have look at this thing. We are not going to ask you to get any more engineering reports because we think you have all the information; will you submit that information to one, two or three experts that we will agree upon and let them tell us whether they are as much convinced as you are?" I have agreed to do that. I think it is a reasonable suggestion and I hope we will be able to get it done before we meet again, even if we meet this fall.

May I make a suggestion to
the minister? Why not take the members of the government out with him and drive from Medicine Hat to Taber and demonstrate to them what has been demonstrated to many of us?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Take the treasury board
along, too.

I would like to do that. In concluding my remarks, I want to say that I do not think I can convince this house or the experts that you can sit down with a pencil and paper and prove that something is going to provide the interest and pay back
Supply-Agriculture
all the money put out on it. But I think I can convince them that twice as many people can live in Saskatchewan if that dam is put in. That means our population will be going up instead of down as it is at present. When I repeat what I said a few moments ago, namely what wheat has meant to the rest of Canada; when I am able to say, as I am convinced, that there will be twice as many people in a certain area to do business with people in other parts of Canada; then I am sure all the rest of Canada will be interested in the building of this dam. My old friend the late John MacNicol used to stand before us in this house and make those of us who came from the west ashamed that we did not have the information he had. He would go out there and walk these streams and study them, and he had every fact at his fingertips. He would tell us what a great thing it would be for the city of Toronto if only we would do this job.
And he was defeated.

As my hon. friend says, he
was defeated; but it was not for that reason, and he had been here a long time. I only mention that tonight because I do not think this is a party matter, or something we ought to be bickering about. I believe it is something we should be trying to get done; and to get it done I think it will be only necessary to put before the members of this house the statement I will place before the government, coming from experts they choose. Then I am sure hon. members will say this will be a good thing for this country.
Does the fact that these experts are going to be called in necessarily mean that the project cannot be proceeded with this year?

Well, we have a million dollars in the estimates. We can continue to spend that, but I do not think we could have gone ahead with the letting of the contract this fall in any case. Hon. members coming from western Canada know that in the letting of a contract on which work can proceed for only six months out in our country, unless you have everything ready at the beginning of the season there is not much use trying to get on with it in that year. We have enough money to put us in the position that if the decision is favourable we can be all ready to go ahead another year. Then if funds are available, if we are not in international difficulties which would slow it up, we can go along just as quickly as if we were to start now.

Have the minister and the government agreed on the experts?

Supply-Agriculture

No, but we have agreed to agree at a later time. I do not think there will be any difficulty about that.
Mr. Cold well:	The minister said he
hoped that before we met again something might be agreed upon.

A name was mentioned today. I do not know the man personally, and I could not very well mention his name here; but I am quite satisfied that the opinion of the gentleman who was named would be generally acceptable in this country.
If the opinion of the experts is favourable this year, could the minister give the committee any assurance that next year construction will definitely commence?

I would not want to do that. So many things are developing these days that one cannot be sure of anything. All I can say is that the government is favourably inclined, as we are all favourably inclined. We just want to be sure on this last point. I think that is reasonable, and I have agreed to it.
I am sure this will be a bitter disappointment to the minister as it will be to the people of Saskatchewan.

I hope the few words I have to say to the minister may be as convincing as what the minister has said to us this evening. First I should like to comment briefly on this irrigation project in the west. I believe all Canadians are anxious to see the natural resources of this country developed to the fullest possible extent, but I am reminded of the tourist who went to Egypt. He was shown the pyramids and was told it took 150 years to build them. His comment was, "Oh, I guess it was a government project". I hope we do not have to wait that long to have this project constructed. There are also those who are a little sceptical, who think the greatest activity seems to occur at about the time of a federal election. After listening to the minister this evening it would seem that about 1952 or 1953 might be the most opportune time to commence this work.
I did not intend to deal with these broad subjects this evening; I wanted to get down to the details of some of the problems affecting the farmers. Since everyone seems to have had something to say about the wheat agreement, however, I might as well mention it also. This is the type of marketing for which the western members have been fighting as long as I can remember, but now they have it they do not want it.
I want to say a word or two about taxation. Taxation affects everyone, but some more

than others. It was Edward Gibbon, the historian, who said that in the final analysis all taxation falls on agriculture. When a tax boost is announced the better organized groups in the country immediately add the tax to the price of the product they sell. We have seen that happen just recently. The less organized groups pass on as much of the tax as possible to the ultimate consumer. Agriculture is in the position that it can add no tax to the price of the product it sells. So no matter what the tax may be on the articles the farmers buy, they have to pay it.
Today I had a complaint from a constituent with respect to the basic herd of a farmer who sells his livestock. I know the minister will say this is a matter for the Department of National Revenue, but I hope he will work in co-operation with that department to bring about a solution to this problem. This man went to his legal adviser and said he was going to have a clearing auction sale of his livestock. He asked about the problem of setting up a basic herd and was advised that it was not necessary to do so, that he could establish that with the income tax department at the conclusion of the sale. Then to his sorrow he found that was too late, that a time limit had been set and that this had to be done at least a month before the auction sale. Now this man finds himself in a position shared by many others in this country. After long years of thrift and industry he is now going to be legally robbed of what was his by the income tax people. It seems to me it would not be a very difficult problem to establish to the satisfaction of the income tax branch the fact that he had twenty or thirty cattle or whatever the number might be during the year or years prior to the auction sale, not just the month before. Now, no other group or class in the country is required to set up a similar workable plan before they sell any article or articles. I would suggest, therefore, that the Minister of National Revenue look into this matter. If an ordinary investor buys stock which he sells after the value has increased, that is a capital gain-unless he happens to be a dealer in stocks or bonds. If I buy real estate and the value increases, when I sell it that is a capital gain.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I believe it would be better to discuss that matter on the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.

I was just referring, sir, to the effect that taxation has on agriculture. I believe I have made the point clear so I shall not press it further, except to say that when livestock is held

over a period of years once the basic herd is established, it is only the increase that is taxable as income. I am asking the department to look into this and see if some change can be made.
I wish to point out also that nearly everyone has been saying something about the cost of living index. I have here a report of the dominion bureau of statistics dated September 22,	1950, over the name of H. F.
Greenway. It is called the "Market Basket" and refers to the requirements of the average family. They take the purchasing power of an hour's labour in 1926 as one. This basket represents, first of all, all living requirements such as food, fuel and light; shelter, rent, clothing, home furnishings and services. Then there is a miscellaneous item which includes health maintenance, personal care, recreation, transportation and insurance. Compared with 1926 an hour's labour in 1939 would buy one-third more of all the living requirements. In 1949 it would buy one and six-tenths more. Of the miscellaneous items, compared with 1926, an hour's labour today will buy almost twice as much as it did in 1926.
Then I come to the Economic Analyst of October, 1950, which gives the average annual market margins on nine selected commodities from 1935 to 1949. In 1935 the margin on potatoes was 9-5 cents on 15 pounds, but in 1949 the margin was 26-6 cents; eggs, all grades, in 1935 the margin was 7-7 per dozen, in 1949 it was 15-4; half-pound packages of cheese, the margin in 1935 was 9 cents, and in 1949 it was 20-4 cents; common quality beef, in 1935 the margin was 6-8 cents per pound and in 1949 it was 17-5. This illustrates where some of the consumers' dollar goes that the farmer does not get. The farmers' share of the retail prices of these same nine selected commodities is given. I shall quote four of them as examples. In 1935 the farmers' share in potatoes was 50 per cent, while in 1949 he only got 49 per cent; in eggs the farmer got 70 per cent of the retail price in 1935, and in 1949 he got 73 per cent; in common quality beef he got 51 1 per cent in 1935 and 64-3 per cent in 1949; in canned tomatoes, in 1935 he got 15-8 per cent and in 1949 he got 20-6 per cent. This shows you, sir, that not all the money the consumer pays finds its way into the pockets of the farmer.
There is one other item I want to mention, and that is the stock foods and tonics that are sold to the farmers for livestock feeding. There are many of these articles processed and manufactured in Canada, but some are imported. It has been proven to my satisfaction that one of the brands contains over
Supply-Agriculture
forty per cent salt, and is sold at fabulous prices. These preparations are in competition with Canadian products that are required to meet higher standards. I discussed this with the Department of Agriculture officials some time ago, but nothing has been done. I hope that before too long this will be looked into by the department and some action taken.

I should like to say a word or two about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act mentioned by the minister. The Minister of Agriculture stated that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was not designed to take care of farmers whose crops were destroyed by hail. Originally, I believe, that was true; but in spite of that he admits that where hail has reduced the yield in any qualified district to eight bushels per acre or less, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does pay some compensation. The minister has stated that anyone can insure his crop against hail, and that he should do so if he is wise. Possibly that point is well taken, but the minister knows that people are inclined to insure only when they feel there is a risk. In the Peace river country damaging hail storms are rare, and for that reason people do not feel that they face a risk. It would not pay the farmers in that part of the country to insure against hail year after year, at least they feel that way, and that is the manner in which they have conducted their affairs. It is only once in a great while that any section of the country is hailed out.
Our biggest hazard, of course, is frost. Sometimes hail and frost come together or one follows the other, so it becomes very difficult to tell which one has caused the yield to fall below the limit to qualify for compensation under the act. I believe, therefore, the minister must admit that it is not a strong argument to say that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should not pay compensation on crops destroyed by hail in an area of that kind, because as I have pointed out the hail there would be just as rare as drought in some other sections.

If I might make myself clear on that point, I am not arguing that there should not be a payment for hail there if there is going to be a payment at all. But I say that merely to argue that the crop was hailed out is not a good reason for bringing the district under the act.

Yes, that is a fair statement, and that is what I was saying. It is not a strong argument against paying compensation. I am sure the minister did not mean it as a strong argument. There was this other point the minister raised. He said that in any district where a crop can be expected in eight

Supp ly-A gricu Iture
out of ten years the farmers ought to be able to take care of themselves in the two bad years when they come. I should be inclined to agree with the minister in that statement if these facts that I shall cite had not been fully established as a result of experience over quite a number of years.
In the first place, in the Peace river country, widespread drought that drastically reduces the yield is only rare. In the second place severe frost and early snow are quite frequent. They are the great hazards, as I have already pointed out. Consequently grades suffer in many years. When grades suffer the returns to the farmers often fall very low. This hits all farmers and it is a serious matter.
The third important point is this. Most farmers whose cases I have been pleading here are comparatively new farmers. They are people who came into the country and took up land under the Alberta crown lease arrangement, covering a period of ten years. The lease arrangement is almost like a ten-year purchase plan. At the end of the ten-year period they got title to these lands. They have had only a few years' experience. Some have had only one, two or three years' experience up there. They have just got started, they are just digging in, as it were. They are facing this situation. In one of the early years of their farming experience in the Peace river country, along comes a tragic or drastic hailstorm, followed by an early frost that reduces the yield in many cases to nothing, and in many of them to much below the qualifying number of bushels. These people are in need. They cannot quite understand why, since they started farming, they should be required to pay the one per cent levy on what crops they market but are not to expect any compensation when their yield falls below eight or four bushels per acre. It is that group I plead for particularly, i would certainly ask the minister to give serious consideration to some change either in the act or in the regulation in order to enable compensation to be paid to them this year. Those people are finding it extremely difficult to meet the cost of putting in their crops-getting seed, buying fuel and repairs to machinery-this year. I should like to ask the minister this question: Has he considered this matter sufficiently to be able to say whether it would be possible to pay compensation on those lands without a change in the act? My feeling is, after studying the act, that it would not be possible. I do not know; I am not an expert.
I must say that I missed the description of the land the hon. member spoke about.
I beg the minister's pardon?
I missed the description of the type of land the hon. member is speaking of, when I was asking my officials for some information.

I merely asked this question. On these crown leases-which as I said amount practically to a ten-year purchase plan- where the farmers are paying in to the government of Alberta a percentage of their crops each year over a period of ten years, and at the end of that period they get their titles, would it be necessary, in the minister's judgment, to change the act before compensation can be paid on such land this year?

My memory is that the act as we amended it last year provided for taking in some areas in the province of Alberta and also, I think, in Saskatchewan, where the lands had been leased by the government; but I think it confines it to those that were leased at a certain period.
Yes; before 1940, I think.
Yes.

I was afraid that would be the case. On lands that were taken in since 1940, it would be impossible for the P.F.A.A. administration to pay compensation for the losses last fall, without a change in the act. If that is the case, is it impossible for the minister to bring in a slight change to the act this year, in order to take care of the situation? I think he will admit that it was not contemplated, when the 1950 amendment was put through, that it would cut off such lands as I have described.

I must say, to be absolutely honest, that it was contemplated. It was not only contemplated but it was discussed in the committee; and after the discussion, it was indicated that we might go along, that after a year's experience we might find that we were doing some things that were not advisable and we might come back for an amendment. What I am saying is that I do not think we would be justified in coming back for an amendment until we have had a year's experience. We have not had the year's experience yet. We should like to go along until the end of the year1.

There is just one thing. I do
not want to labour this point, but in referring to the amendment the minister himself made this important point, as reported at page 3310 of Hansard of 1950:
I want to make it perfectly plain that the bill-
I am speaking now of the amending bill in 1950.
-does not deal with submarginal lands as such. It deals with lands which up to a certain date every-

body considered were not good enough either to homestead or to buy. It is true that having set the date at December 31, 1940, there will be a few pieces of land in Saskatchewan particularly that were homesteaded after that date, and there will be a few parcels that were purchased after that date but they are largely in areas where the act would not apply in any case.
All of that I think has reference to submarginal lands and lands in drier areas.

That particular discussion
that is referred to there had a bearing on the area that was settled in the south. There is no question about that.

The point I was trying to make was that actually in all the discussions that took place-and I thought I got fairly close to it here-there was no mention of lands of the type I have described to the minister up in the Peace river country.
There was in Saskatchewan. There was mention of that type of land in Saskatchewan.

I want to say that I was much amazed to hear the statement of the Minister of Agriculture with respect to the South Saskatchewan river dam. Up until well into the body of his speech I had hoped that an announcement might be forthcoming that construction would take place immediately. I can remember back in 1947 when the minister told us in this house that it would take two years from 1947 to decide whether the project was feasible or not. Then in the 1949 election the minister himself said to the people of Saskatchewan to send him back to complete the job. Then in the first session after that election the minister said: The Saskatchewan government has to pay some $30 million, and we do not know whether or not they are going to do that. Those were brand new conditions, but the Saskatchewan government has met those conditions. I see by the press that the latest survey made on that project says that it is feasible. Yet the minister gets up in the house tonight and says that a brand new survey is going to have to be made by a brand new set of engineers. Then he is asked whether when that survey is made-
That is not correct.
A brand new set of experts.
No, no. There is no survey going to be made at all.
What are they going to do?

A survey that has been
made is going to be submitted to a few experts, to get their opinion.

I know that my hon. friend is preparing for a by-election in his area. He is not satisfied with what other members of his own party were inclined to agree with a few minutes ago.
What was that?
He just does not want this thing settled. He has just got through saying-

Mr. Chairman, the minister has accused me of preparing for a by-election in my area. I am fighting for the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam. I think it is a good thing for the province of Saskatchewan, and he should not suggest that I am doing it for political purposes.

It is quite all right. On a question of privilege, what I want to point out is that my hon. friend just got through saying that toward the end of 1947 I had said there was two years' work still to be done before anyone could be convinced as to whether or not it should be proceeded with. This is still early in 1951. If it took two years to convince me, and others who were close to it, as to whether it could be successfully gone ahead with, we are not very far off the line that was laid out at that time. As a matter of fact, when you add the sessions together we are quite within reasonable distance of the time. I was convinced at the end of the two years. I think I have indicated to the committee tonight that I am convinced. There are a few others that I have to convince. There are ways of doing that, and I do not want somebody to tell me, because it would be true if they did, that I am not an engineer and do not know whether we could make

that dam stay there or not; or that I do not know whether the water can be successfully utilized for power after it is over. Some of the people who have been quoted tonight as being absolutely satisfied have stated to me that you can produce power there cheaper with coal than you can with water. I do not agree with them, but it has had the effect of making some people wonder. I am so far convinced about the matter myself that I am quite satisfied all the facts should be submitted to experts, and I think the experts will come to the same conclusion that I have come to.
The minister's arithmetic is not too good. In 1947 he said it would take two years to find out.
At the end of 1947.
If I can add, the period from 1947 to 1949 amounts to two years. All right; the minister has just said that it was feasible.
I was convinced.
This is 1951, and he is still trying to convince the members of the government that it is feasible. He has not convinced them today.

I will agree with my hon. friend excepting for the one word he uses. He says that because I am convinced, I know. Well, I may think that I know, but there may be other people who think that I do not know. I am convinced.
He has been convinced since 1949, and he has not convinced any member of the government.
Oh, no; don't go that far.

He says that there is disagreement. He took one position and the treasury board or some other members of the government took another position. From 1949 to 1951 is two years, and in that time he has not convinced the members of the government; he has not convinced anybody. Now it is going to go to some experts. They are going to go over all the surveys, and the Minister of Agriculture cannot say, even when that is done, whether or not construction will start next year, if the decision is favourable.
If I did, the hon. member would say: there is an election coming up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

That shows the mind of the minister. He knows, and he will not be prepared to say construction will take place until just before another election. He said 
in 1949, on the eve of the election, as quoted in the Regina Leader-Post of June 23, 1949, and I am quoting from the speech he made at Lemberg, Saskatchewan:
"The South Saskatchewan project would provide cheap power and encourage building of industries in small towns, provide an incentive for young people to stay in this province. I think we have made a fairly good start now," said Mr. Gardiner. "Send us back to complete the job . . ."
Sure, and they did, too.
They were sent back to complete the job, and two years later the minister is still having a survey made. He is no further ahead than he was in 1949.
No, that is not right.

It is not good enough for the Minister of Agriculture to say to the people of Saskatchewan in 1949: Send me back and I will complete the job, and then two years later to be doing nothing toward the completion of the job, and not be able to say that construction on that project will even commence next year.
I intend to make my remarks very brief. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is one time that I can speak in this house without being critical of our dominion government on their irrigation program.
Have they an irrigation program in Alberta? Did they build an irrigation project there?
You should come out and see it.
It is oil that has done that.

I must say that through the co-operation of the dominion government and of our good friend the Minister of Agriculture and our provincial government we have irrigation within sight of Medicine Hat. I hope when the minister comes out in two years' time or three years, or perhaps even at election time, we shall have the water in those ditches just west of Medicine Hat so that it will not be necessary to drive to Taber to see the change in the country and the change that water can make when it is put on land such as we have in that area.
Irrigation means so much to our western provinces, not only to Alberta but to Saskatchewan and perhaps to some parts of Manitoba as well. I might say that perhaps in Alberta we are situated in the driver's seat. We have the water there not only for the St. Mary-Milk river project but for the Bow river development project, which has been taken over by the dominion government. We have a few small projects. One I might mention is the Ross creek irrigation project, a project which will bring under

water 2,500 acres of land. I do not want to say any more about that at the present time because I have one or two questions I want to ask the minister when we get on to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
On occasion the minister has wondered why so many people stay on the dry lands surrounding Medicine Hat. The minister knows the answer just as well as I do. There they have been waiting to utilize water that is running down and being wasted in the South Saskatchewan river. We have come to realize that that water must be used, not only to the advantage of the -settlers on the land but to the advantage of the cities, and not only to the advantage of the cities but to that of both senior governments. Because we all realize that when we put water on the land that land can be reassessed at a better value. Land assessed at $1 an acre today may be assessed at $30 when water is put on. So that we can all benefit by it.
I am very happy at this time to compliment the Minister of Agriculture and his government, and I am mighty happy to compliment the Social Credit government in Alberta upon co-operating with the dominion government to make the irrigation project possible.

I wish that at this time I could compliment the Minister of Agriculture upon the job he has done so far as irrigation in Saskatchewan is concerned. I am very sorry however that I cannot, because tonight he has made an announcement that will shock the people in the whole of that province.
I cannot help going back to the first time I ran in a federal election in 1945. I remember the leading newspaper advertisement carried by my political opponent, a whole page in our local newspaper, saying, "South Saskatchewan irrigation project has been approved; it will be commenced as soon as men and material are available." That was in 1945.
As I said earlier today, every year goes by and some other reason is found for not proceeding with it. Tonight we heard the minister give a very interesting speech on what had been accomplished in Alberta. He said that where formerly we had a dust bowl we now have tree belts and springs, and that everything is growing. He said that was why he wanted to sell the committee on the proposition of doing something similar in Saskatchewan.
Well, everyone will agree that there are advantages; but we would like to know why some action is not being taken this year. Whom could not the minister sell? Tonight we had another illustration that there is some

I said a moment ago that I do not think the minister's explanation holds water; it is not good enough. It may be that I am biased; but I say now that this dam is being held until the year before the next federal election, so that the minister can go to the people of Saskatchewan, and say that he is starting. I regret that I cannot, like the hon. member for Medicine Hat, compliment the minister tonight, because regardless of their politics our people are bitterly disappointed.

They were run at a loss and finally closed up. Men who did not know beans about business had tried to run them. I am not referring to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). I think he is in strange company because he himself is a capitalist and is interested in four paying concerns.
In so far as the Minister of Agriculture and this whole dam proposition is concerned, I think the government will be convinced. Those of us who have travelled from Red Deer across the United States border down through Idaho and have seen what has been done with irrigation have some idea what can be done in our part of the country. I think all of Canada will be behind this project. I cannot imagine members in eastern Canada bucking western prosperity.

Mr. Chairman, I had to attend the veterans affairs committee this afternoon but I am told there was considerable discussion in this committee this afternoon with regard to wheat. This evening I heard the minister replying to statements that had been made this afternoon. The minister warned hon. members who were supporters of the wheat board and long-term international wheat agreements that they should be careful in criticizing these institutions because it might weaken them. I want to make it quite clear that I am a one hundred per cent supporter of the wheat board and of long-term international wheat agreements but I think it necessary at times to point out any weaknesses that may develop.
This afternoon the minister pointed out that there was no provision in the international wheat agreement under which the ceiling or floor price could be changed during

the term of the contract. I agree that that is right, but I would point out that back in 1948 and 1949 when the agreement was up for discussion in the house I urged the government to try to get the price of wheat tied to the price level so that if in the future the general price level went up, the price of wheat would go up, and if the price level went down, the price of wheat would go down.
If that had been done we would have avoided the criticism that we hear today that the world price of wheat is $2.28 per bushel while wheat sold under the international wheat agreement returns only $1.89. Personally I do not think there would be any difficulty making an arrangement of that kind. Certainly the price for the first year of the agreement could be arranged without any difficulty and then the future prices could be tied to the price level. That would be of advantage to both the selling and the buying nations.
Apparently the government did not advocate that at the time the international wheat agreement was signed, and apparently the farmer organizations did not ask for that. It is quite evident today that the farmer organizations are realizing that a'provision of that kind should be introduced' into the wheat agreement and they are now asking for an escalator clause. When the present international wheat agreement expires I hope the government will try to have some form of escalator clause included in the agreement.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was referring to the marketing of wheat during the past five years he stated that in that time the farmers had received a better return for their wheat than in any other five-year period in the history of Canada. That statement is not quite correct. The only period in the history of Canada during which the farmer received a parity price was the five-year period 1916-20. During that period the farm population represented one-third of the population of the country and the farm income was approximately one-third of the total income of Canada. So at that time the farmer actually received a parity price for his farm production.
Having that in mind I asked the bureau of statistics to prepare me some index figures, using 1916-20 as 100. I asked for index figures on wheat prices and prices of farm machinery for the period 1925-29, which is often referred to as being a period of prosperity for agriculture, and also the period 1945-50, which was referred to by the minister. The figures are quite interesting because they show clearly that the farmer

There is just one other point I should like to refer to before eleven o'clock, the matter of irrigation. I want to say to the minister that the farmers of Acadia constituency very much appreciate the work that has been done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, that is, the building of dugouts and dams on various creeks for irrigation purposes. A number of fairly large dams have been constructed on Berry creek and Sounding creek with the idea of impounding waters to irrigate quite a considerable area of land. Unfortunately, owing to an insufficient runoff of water, until this year there has been very little water in those dams and irrigation could not be carried on. This spring, however, the dams were overflowing. We had a fine runoff of water, and there will be enough to provide for quite a large amount of irrigation. That irrigation will have to be done by sprinkler systems; there is no other way it can be carried on with the type of dams we have built, and of course sprinkler equipment is quite expensive. It is not going to be easy for many farmers to obtain the equipment necessary to irrigate their land; but the eastern irrigation association are working to get farmers to co-operate with one another and provide sprinklers so a real trial of the system can be carried out in that area.
Of course the irrigation scheme the farmers of Acadia are really interested in is the Red Deer diversion project. When that is

Supply-Agriculture
finally completed it will provide a steady supply of water to be carried to the dams already built on Berry creek and Sounding creek. Last year the minister said he hoped that by the fall of 1950 the surveys for the Red river project would have advanced sufficiently to make it possible to sign an agreement with the provincial government. Could the minister, either tonight or when we come to the item on irrigation, say just what the situation is?
Perhaps it would be better to leave it until we reach the item.

That will be quite satisfactory. When I travelled through the constituency I told the farmers what the minister had said, but I warned that because of the international situation it was quite possible the government would have to curtail expenditures on some irrigation projects in order to provide for greater expenditures for war purposes. The farmers are reasonable; they realize the situation, and they will not be over-critical if the government is not able to proceed right away. However, good progress has been made with the surveys, and the farmers are now using the dams
already built for small-scale irrigation. They realize that if they show the government they can make good use of the water already provided the government will be more likely to provide additional water in the future.
